en: Susiddhikara Sūtra, Volume One. Translated by the Tripitaka Master Śubhakarasiṃha of India during the Tang Dynasty. Chapter One: The Chapter on Inquiry. **Chapter One: The Chapter on Inquiry** At that time, the World-Honored One was dwelling in the great city of Vārāṇasī, in the Deer Park at Ṛṣipatana, together with a great assembly of monks and a great assembly of bodhisattvas. At that time, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Susiddhi, having risen from his seat, arranged his robes over one shoulder, knelt with his right knee on the ground, joined his palms toward the Buddha, and addressed him, saying: “World-Honored One, I now wish to ask about the secret mantras and the rituals for their accomplishment. May the Tathāgata, out of compassion, explain them for me. The Buddha said to the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Susiddhi: “Excellent, excellent! Son of good family, you have asked well. Listen attentively and bear it in mind; I shall now explain for you the secret mantras and the rituals for their accomplishment. The Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Susiddhi replied to the Buddha: “I shall listen attentively and bear it in mind according to the instructions of the Buddha. The Buddha then spoke these verses: “Listen, O son of good family, to the supreme secret mantras. They are the source of all accomplishments and the root of all dharmas. If one wishes to attain the fruit of the Great Vehicle, One must first seek the path of the Secret Mantra Vehicle. The mantras are of three kinds: those of the Buddhas, Those of the Bodhisattvas, and those of the Vidyādharas. Each has its own specific ritual procedures and methods of accomplishment. Now I shall explain them in detail for you. [End of Chapter One] *Note: The text provided consists of the title and introductory section of the first chapter of the Susiddhikara Sūtra.*
At that time, the Bodhisattva Krodha-Caṇḍālī joined her palms in reverence, prostrated at the feet of the Venerable Vajrapāṇi, and asked this question:

"In the past, I have already inquired of the Venerable One regarding the various vidyārāja maṇḍala rites and their sequential procedures, as well as having heard of the miraculous efficacy and virtues of the vidyārājas and their retinues. I pray that the Venerable One will explain them extensively for the sake of all sentient beings of the future; I pray that the Venerable One will provide a detailed exposition on which ritual methods and sequence of mantra recitation will lead to swift accomplishment."
Although the methods for requesting mantras are of a single essence, the number of things to be accomplished by them is immeasurable.
What are the characteristics of a mantra? What is an ācārya?
What constitutes a disciple who has achieved accomplishment?
What place is considered a superior site?
And how does one swiftly achieve accomplishment through mantras?
What are the characteristics of subduing?
What are the methods and sequences for reciting mantras?
And what is the offering of flowers?
How are the unguents used?
How is the food offered?
Furthermore, what kind of incense is burned?
What are the characteristics of the Illumination rite?
What is the Śāntika rite?
And what are the characteristics of the Puṣṭika rite?
How does one subdue the enemy?
Among these three types, what specific matters are accomplished by each?
What are the characteristics of their superior, middling, and inferior sequential accomplishments?
By what dharma is one summoned?
How is one to make offerings?
And how does one perform the protection of the body?
How does one extensively perform recitation?
What are the characteristics by which a mantra is attained?
And what is the ritual procedure for performing the consecration of mantras?
How should one receive the entrustment?
How are the syllables fulfilled? How is there increase?
How does one perform the homa and its sequential rites?
Furthermore, by using what substances can one achieve swift accomplishment?
And what are the characteristics of the perfected medicinal elixir?
How does one purify and maintain the medicines?
What is the prescribed dosage of the medicines?
And what are the characteristics of the various medicines?
How are the characteristics of all things accomplished?
How are the characteristics of all things received?
How can the dharmas of all things be purified?
What is the measure and quantity of these things?
Regarding those various objects and their characteristics, I pray that the Venerable One, endowed with great compassion, will explain each one clearly for me.
How are the various accomplished substances (*siddhadravya*) protected and categorized?
How are these accomplished substances utilized?
We pray that you will compassionately explain this in detail.
How does one recover lost objects?
How does one cause those who have been defeated to submit once more?
And how does one first recognize the signs of impending obstacles?
What is the accomplishment of the maṇḍala?
What is the maṇḍala of ritual characteristics?
What is the maṇḍala of empowerment?

Regarding the essential points of the questions as they have been followed above, I only pray that the Venerable One, out of great compassion for the sake of sentient beings, will compassionately analyze and explain them in detail.

2. The Section on the Characteristics of Mantras, Part Two. At that time, the Great Holy One, the Holder of the Vajra, the Auspiciously Adorned Sovereign of All Vidyādharas and Object of Worship, addressed the Bodhisattva Mahāvīra Krodha (Great Heroic Wrath):
“Excellent, excellent!”
"O Great Wrathful One!
Since you have been able to pose such a question to me, you should listen with single-minded attention to this most supreme, profound, and secret wondrous Dharma.
This *Susiddhikara Sūtra* possesses five kinds of adornments."
First, it is called Great Diligence;
second, it is called the Vidyārāja;
third, it is able to eliminate obstacles.
Fourth, it can accomplish all fierce rites;
fifth, it can accomplish all mantras.

Regarding this *Susiddhikara Sūtra*, if there are those who recite other true dharmas and mantras without success, they should be made to concurrently hold the root mantra of this sūtra, and they shall then swiftly achieve the methods of all mantras.
Among the three families, this sūtra is the principal one; it is also capable of accomplishing all matters, namely:

protecting the body, binding the boundary, summoning, making offerings, providing assistance, inflicting punishment, and giving instructions. It enables each and every mantra to achieve success in its respective sequence.
Furthermore, within certain heart-mantras (hṛdaya-mantra), the three syllables "huṃ" are likewise capable of accomplishing all the ritual activities described above.
The heart-mantra consisting of the three "huṃ" syllables is as follows:

“*Namo ratnatrayāya, namo mañjuśriye vajrapāṇaye mahā-uccaṭṭaseṇapataye. Oṃ siddhya siddhya svāhā susiddhikara hūṃ hūṃ hūṃ ṭaṭa ṭaṭa.*” Furthermore, regarding the methods for superior, middling, and inferior accomplishments as taught in other sūtras, those who wish to achieve accomplishments such as *praṇidhāna* (vows) should understand the superior, middling, and inferior methods of mantras.
This *Susiddhikara Sūtra* comprehensively encompasses the maṇḍala rites performed by the three families:
the śāntika rite using mantras of the Buddha family;
and the pauṣṭika rite using mantras of the Lotus family.
Regarding the *ābhicāruka* rites of the Vajra Family mantras:
from the armpits to the crown of the head is the superior [level]; from the navel to the armpits is the middling; and from the feet to the navel is the inferior.

Within the mantras, one should also distinguish three types of accomplishment (*siddhi*). Each of these three families (*kula*) is further divided into three; one should understand and discern them well.
Among the various mantras of those three families, the mantras of the Vidyārājas constitute the superior accomplishment;
the mantras of the other messengers (*dūta*), *ceta*, *cetaka*, and so forth, constitute the inferior accomplishment.
"The three types of ritual methods are:
first, śāntika; second, pauṣṭika;"
Third, ābhicāruka.
Thus, within each of the three families, there are three types of these matters; one must thoroughly understand their sequential characteristics.
"Within the Buddha Family, one employs the Buddha-Mother, known as Buddhalocanā; using this mantra performs the śāntika rite.
The mantra of the Buddha-Mother is as follows:
*Namo bhagavate uṣṇīṣāya | oṃ ru ru sphuru jvali tiṣṭha siddha | locane sarvārthasādhani | svāhā* This is the mantra of the Mother of the Buddha Family, namely Buddhalocanā."
"In the Lotus Family, there is the Mother of Avalokiteśvara known as Pañcarakṣā; this mantra is used for śāntika rites.
The mantra of the Mother of Avalokiteśvara is as follows:"

“*Narśaṃ saṃprāśaṃ raśanaṃ praśīrva saṃrāṇe na ca kṣa maṃha sarvasattvānāṃ sarvavidhi cikitsaka oṃ vikhaṭa kaṭa vikhaṭa kaṭiṅkaṭa kahe vaghavati vraye svāhā.*” This is the mantra of the Mother of the Lotus Family (*padmakulamātṛmantra*), which is *paṇḍaravāsini*.
"In the Vajra Family, one employs the Vajrī Māmakī, known as Māmakī; using this mantra for *śāntika* rites.
The mantra of the Mother of the Vajra Family is:
*Namo ratnatrayāya | namo mañjuśriye vajrapāṇaye mahāyakṣasenāpataye | oṃ kulanandari bandha bandha hūṃ phaṭ |" [Recite] three times.
This is the mantra of Vajrayoginī, namely *Māmakī*.
Furthermore, within the Buddha Family (*buddhakula*), one employs the mantra of a Vidyārāja.
This Vidyārāja is named Uṣṇīṣavijaya; one employs this mantra for the purpose of *puṣṭika* (nourishment).
The mantra of the Vidyārāja is:
"Na-maḥ samantabuddhānām | oṃ bhrūṃ na-maḥ. Within the Lotus Family, there is also a Vidyārāja named Hayagrīva; this mantra is used for pauṣṭika rites.
The mantra of the Vidyārāja is:
“Oṃ jambutu-pa-va-nam-maṃ svāhā. Within the Vajra Family, there is also a Vidyārāja named Subha; this mantra is used for pauṣṭika rites.
The mantra is: "Namaḥ ratnatrayāya."
NAMAḤ ŚRĪVAJRAPĀṆAYE.
Maṅkhaghuśeṣacintāpate oṃ soḥ bhaḥ.
Oṃ hūṃ phreṃ haṃ niḥ.
PHREṂ HŪṂ PHREṂ HŪṂ
Hūṃ ākara-ya-huḥ.
Bhagavān Vajrin Hūṃ.
"Ṭaṅ maṃ. Furthermore, within the Mother Tantra (Buddhamātṛ-tantra), one employs the Great Wrathful One known as Aparājita; this mantra is used for the rite of Abhicāruka.
The mantra is:
"HŪṂ HṢṬA DĪKA DĪKA DĪKA KARA SARVA KĀRYĀṆI HŪṂ HṢṬA. This is the Great Wrathful One within the Lotus Family, named Śvāsa; one employs this mantra for *abhicāruka* rites.
The mantra is:
"HŪṂ HṚT ĀRI HŪṂ HṚT. This is the Great Wrathful One of the Vajra Family, named Kuṇḍalī; this mantra is used for the *ābhicāruka* rite.
The mantra is: "Namo ratnatrayāya."
NAMAḤ ŚRĪCAṆḌAVAJRAPĀṆYE.
Mahāyakṣasenāpate oṃ jayapratāpa-kumāra.
Kha kha khakhe
khāḍi ṭiṣṭha ṭiṣṭha.
Panthā panthānaḥ pathaḥ pathāḥ.
Viṣphuṭaya viṣphuṭaya sarva-...
Near the tail is the subtle sac;
*khaṃ mahā-śrī-patir-ni-dantaka-rāja*.
"Hūṃ phaṭ.

Furthermore, there may be mantras that do not belong to the three families; one should distinguish the three types of ritual activities, such as śāntika and so forth, according to the syllables of those respective mantras.
If within a mantra there are the syllables "śāntikaru," "svastikuṇu," "cuṃ," "pracuṃ," "upacuṃ," or "svāhā," one should know that it is a śāntika mantra.

"If there are the syllables *puṣpakuṃkuma*, *rakṣa mama*, *ūrjū*, *māra*, *vāridhi*, *ambha*, *medha*, *tana tani*, *helini*, *garāma*, *nagarā*, *rasta*, *rardhyannana*, and *namo namaḥ*, one should know that these constitute the mantra of Śaṅkhinī."

"If there are the syllables *hūṃ*, *hana*, *phaṭ*, *manta*, *vajra*, *rātya*, *ucāṭana*, *śoṣaṇamāra*, *kṣepaṇa*, *āla*, *cchedana*, and *vāsikye kuru*, one should know that these are the mantras of the ābhicāruka [rite]."
"Furthermore, if there is a mantra whose words and meaning are benevolent and compassionate, one should know that it pertains to the function of *śāntika* (pacification);
if there is a mantra whose words and meaning are fierce and wrathful, one should know that it pertains to the function of *abhicāruka* (subjugation/terrible rites);
if there is a mantra that is neither fierce [nor benevolent], one should know that it pertains to the function of *pauṣṭika* (nourishment/enrichment)."
"Furthermore, if one wishes to swiftly accomplish *śāntika*, one should employ the mantras of the Buddha Family;
if one wishes to swiftly accomplish *pauṣṭika*, one should employ the mantras of the Lotus Family;
if one wishes to swiftly accomplish *abhicāruka*, one should employ the mantras of the Vajra Family."

"Furthermore, this sutra is profound and subtle like the God among Gods; it also possesses mantras of superior, middling, and inferior grades. If one relies upon these methods, there is no task whatsoever that will not be accomplished."

Although this sūtra belongs to the third division, the Vajra Family (Vajrakula), because it has been granted permission by the Buddha's command to be practiced universally, it can also accomplish the practices of the two higher divisions.
It is just as when a king grants permission; practicing this rite in accordance with that authorization is likewise effective.

"According to this principle, it should be understood that even if a mantra consists of many syllables, if it begins with the syllable 'Oṃ' and ends with the syllable 'Svāhā,' one should know that this mantra can swiftly accomplish the *śāntika* rite;
or if there is a mantra that begins with the syllable 'Hūṃ' and ends with the syllable 'Phaṭ';"
There may be mantras containing the syllable *hauṃ*—this is a word-sound—and those possessing such syllables as these will swiftly achieve the *abhicāruka* rite.

Alternatively, there may be mantras that lack the syllable *oṃ* at the beginning, lack the syllable *svāhā* at the end, and further lack the syllable *hūṃ*, as well as the syllable *phaṭ* and syllables such as *hauṃ*; one should know that such mantras are capable of swiftly accomplishing the *pauṣṭika* rite.
"If there is anyone who wishes to subdue various other spirits and *piśācas*, they shall quickly attain accomplishment by using the mantras spoken by the *dūtas* and *ceṭakas*.
If there are mantras from other sections (*kula*) said to be able to accomplish all matters, they can only accomplish what is taught within their own section and do not apply to other sections."

Furthermore, there are sūtras that expound mantras for the purpose of eliminating poison and disease; therefore, when it is said that they cannot eliminate other types of suffering, one should understand that this applies to all general uses.
One must well know the respective classes [of mantras], well recognize the appropriate applications of the mantras, and also understand the power of the mantras;

furthermore, one must skillfully comprehend the methods for cultivating mantra-practice, such that according to the matter sought, one accords with the characteristics of the corresponding mantra-dharma, and by reciting that mantra, accomplishment is attained.

3. Chapter on Distinguishing the Characteristics of the Ācārya. Susiddhikara, Chapter Three: Distinguishing the Characteristics of the Ācārya. "Furthermore, I shall now explain the characteristics of the ācārya."
All mantras are obtained from him; therefore, it should be clearly understood that the ācārya is the most fundamental.
What are his characteristics? They are as follows:
With all limbs complete and adorned with merit;
skillfully understanding all mundane and supramundane phenomena;
and always abiding in accordance with the Dharma, never practicing what is contrary to the Dharma.
Possessing great compassion and pitying sentient beings;
born into a noble and eminent lineage, he is disciplined and gentle;
and wherever he dwells with others, all obtain peace and happiness.
They possess intelligence, wisdom, and unimpeded eloquence;
they are able to maintain patience and are free from conceit;
they always delight in the Mahāyāna and understand its profound meaning.
Furthermore, one should have deep faith and delight in the gateway of the secret [mantras];
even for minor transgressions, one should maintain great trepidation;
and one must properly cultivate the flexibility and gentleness of the actions of body, speech, and mind.
One should always delight in reciting and reading Mahāyāna sūtras,
and furthermore, diligently chant mantras according to the scriptural teachings without interruption;
thus, all sought-after siddhis will be fully accomplished.
Furthermore, one must be skilled in drawing maṇḍalas, always possess the four means of attraction (saṃgrahavastu),
seek the Great [Vehicle] rather than delighting in minor conditions, be forever free from stinginess,
and have previously entered a great maṇḍala to receive empowerment (abhiṣeka).
Furthermore, one should praise the virtues of one's former teacher, saying:
"From this day forward, you are worthy to bestow the empowerment and serve as an ācārya.

Having received this authorization, it is appropriate for you to personally construct the maṇḍala according to the prescribed sequence, and it is likewise appropriate that you confer the mantras upon your disciples.
If one relies upon this, the mantras one receives will swiftly attain accomplishment; one must not harbor doubts.
If one recites mantras at will without being under the guidance of such an ācārya as described above, one will merely expend effort in vain and ultimately fail to obtain the fruit.
“The dharma for a disciple is to regard the ācārya as being like the Three Jewels and the Bodhisattvas, for he is the one capable of bestowing the refuge.

He is the primary cause for all virtuous deeds; through reliance upon the ācārya, one attains peace and happiness in the present life and reaps the fruits in the future, and before long, one shall attain the unsurpassed and supreme state, which is bodhi.”

For this reason, one should regard [the teacher] as a Buddha and serve him as a disciple serves an ācārya, being diligent and unwearied, never failing to uphold [his instructions]. If one receives from him the vidyārāja or vidyārājñī, one will certainly attain siddhi; of this there is no doubt.
Chapter Four: Distinguishing the Characteristics of Mantra Recitation Furthermore, I shall now expound the characteristics of the method for reciting mantras to swiftly attain accomplishment.
The three karmas are pure and the mind is undistracted;
one constantly cultivates wisdom without interruption;
and being able to practice a single dharma that accomplishes all matters, one is further free from stinginess and greed.
The words they utter are free from impediment;
they dwell among the assembly without fear and accomplish their tasks with speed;
they constantly practice patience and remain free from all flattery and deceit.
They shall be free from all diseases;
they shall always practice truthful speech and understand the matters of wholesome dharmas;
and in their youth, their years, their faculties, and their physical limbs shall all be perfectly complete.
One should constantly give rise to faith toward the Triple Gem;
practice the subtle and wondrous Mahāyāna sūtras, and never harbor thoughts of retreat regarding any virtuous merit—such a person will swiftly achieve accomplishment.
"One who constantly maintains reverence for all bodhisattvas and mantras,
and gives rise to great compassion for all sentient beings— such a person will swiftly attain accomplishment."

"One who constantly delights in tranquility and does not dwell among disturbances, who always practices truthful speech and maintains a mind of pure protection—such a person will swiftly attain accomplishment.
If one hears of the power of the Vajra and attains mastery of the body, and immediately gives rise to joy through sincere faith—such a person will swiftly attain accomplishment."
"If a person has few desires and is content, reciting and upholding the mantra while contemplating their goal day and night without ceasing, such a person will swiftly attain accomplishment."

"If a person, upon first hearing the rules of the mantra-dharma, has their body hairs stand on end and their heart is filled with leaping joy and delight, such a person is a vessel for accomplishment."

"If a person sees their own siddhi in a dream as described in the sūtras, and delights in mental tranquility rather than dwelling among the multitude, such a person will swiftly attain accomplishment."
"If there is another person who honors and respects the ācārya as they would the Buddha, such a person will swiftly attain accomplishment.

If a person recites a mantra for a long time without obtaining results, they must not abandon it; rather, they should redouble their vows, increase their diligence, and continue until success is achieved—such a person will swiftly attain accomplishment."

Chapter Five: Distinguishing the Characteristics of Companions. From the Susiddhikara Sūtra, Chapter Five: Distinguishing the Characteristics of Companions. "Furthermore, I shall now explain the characteristics of those companions.
Born into a noble family of merit and virtue;
always delighting in the True Dharma and not practicing what is contrary to it;
furthermore, harboring deep faith and being free from all fears, they are diligent and do not regress.
He upholds the Honored One’s teachings and always speaks truthful words;
all his faculties and limbs are perfectly complete and his body is free from disease;
he is neither too tall nor too short, neither too stout nor too emaciated, and neither too dark nor too fair—thus he is free from such defects.
Having merit as one's companion, being able to endure all sufferings;
being well-versed in the mantras and the ritual procedures for mandala offerings and other dharmas;
and constantly practicing the pure conduct (brahmacarya) in accordance with all matters.
His speech is gentle and pleasant for others to hear;
he is free from all conceit;
and he possesses a powerful memory that never forgets.
One should practice what one has received without making excuses;
possessing much learning and wisdom, one should further possess compassion and constantly mindfully practice giving;
being skilled in discernment, one must always recite the mantras of the Vidyārāja.
The mantra one holds should be identical to the practice of the Honored One;
furthermore, one must clearly understand the methods for binding the boundary (*sīmābandha*) and protecting the body (*kāyarakṣā*). With such companions, one shall swiftly attain accomplishment.
"The three karmas are well-disciplined;..."
Having entered the maṇḍala in the presence of the master;
having taken refuge in the Buddha's teachings and not practicing heterodox dharmas;
and being well-versed in the proper sequence of what the Venerable One requires.
Without needing verbal instruction, whenever one seeks anything, they provide it immediately; one who possesses such qualities is a superior companion.
With body and mind virtuous, free from anxiety and affliction, resolute and firm with no intention to retreat—one who obtains such a companion shall swiftly achieve accomplishment.
"One who does not give rise to greedy attachment toward abundant wealth and profit, and who possesses such virtues, is called an excellent companion.

Furthermore, one whose mind never abandons the practitioner—even when seeking to accomplish other medicinal substances and the like—acts as a powerful condition for their success and should not be abandoned; possessing such natural noble precepts and such virtues, they are called an excellent companion."

"One should have no expectations or desires regarding the practitioner; until the attainment of *siddhi* is achieved, one must never abandon them. Even if many years pass without *siddhi*, one should never harbor a thought of abandonment. Even if great suffering or other hardships press upon the body and mind, one should not forsake them. One endowed with such virtues is called an excellent companion."

"If there are those who possess various virtues as previously described and are capable of accomplishing the most supreme and excellent matters, even if they lack those virtues, provided they clearly understand the ritual rules for mantra accomplishment, are well-versed in the wisdom of all maṇḍalas, and are further distinguished by superior diligence and recitation—such companions can also accomplish the most supreme and excellent matters."

"In order to accomplish the most supreme and excellent matters of one's aspirations, his merit and virtue shall act as companions to the practitioner, bestowing empowerments (*abhiṣeka*) and performing *homa* offerings every half-month. At all times, they shall provide whatever incense, flowers, and lamps are prepared, as well as carry out all other successive rites of protection and discernment; whatever is required, they must assist in its execution."

Not only does such a companion assist in the practice as described above in honoring the Honored One, but if the practitioner should suffer any deficiency or loss, this companion of merit shall instruct them according to the principles of the sūtras and the Dharma so that no omission occurs; even going so far as to extensively explain the underlying causes and conditions—one who possesses such qualities is the most excellent companion.

"When a practitioner recites daily or performs their practices and happens to forget something, this merit will accompany them wherever they go, assisting them in performing those tasks so that everything becomes complete."
When one wishes to accomplish the medicinal rites, one must constantly press the medicine with the hand or use a stalk of grass to press it.
Although the ritual activities of recitation may be numerous, the practitioner must not neglect or forget the mantra recitation.

When one intends to conclude [the recitation], the companion must stand nearby; observing whether that Venerable One has become fatigued from the chanting, or fearing that he might forget to perform the ritual for dispatching the deities, the ritual for setting aside the rosary, or other such rites, one should assist him in performing whatever he is seen to have forgotten.

"One's companion must constantly maintain recitation and perform offerings for all activities undertaken, so that the resulting merit may be dedicated toward fulfilling the aspirations of the mantra-holder. When receiving instructions, one should speak only with the companion; since one seeks to accomplish the most supreme matters, it is further permitted to have one companion with whom one may converse in turn, provided there is no discord."

"The food consumed by his companion is the same as that of the Venerable One; not only do they eat together, but he also ensures that what is held and what is eaten is in accordance with the established rules. One who possesses such qualities is fit to be a companion for the most supreme and excellent task."
The second companion and the third companion are likewise, exactly as previously described. Chapter Six:

Selection of the Site From the Susiddhikara Sūtra, Chapter Six: Selection of the Site Furthermore, I shall now explain the locations for the accomplishment of mantra recitation: in which place must one dwell to swiftly attain accomplishment?
The place where the Buddha attained enlightenment and subdued the four Māras is the most supreme among such locations for swiftly attaining accomplishment (*siddhi*).

Because there are no obstacles on the banks of the Nairañjanā River, one will swiftly attain *siddhi* at that site; even if obstacles should arise, they cannot act as hindrances, and whatever is sought will be accomplished without fail—one will swiftly attain accomplishment at such a place.
Alternatively, it may be at the site where the Buddha turned the Wheel of Dharma.
Alternatively, at the site of the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa in the city of Kuśinagara,
or at the place of the Buddha’s birth in the city of Kapilavastu—
these four aforementioned locations are the most excellent and superior; because they are free from obstacles and disturbances, the three kinds of siddhi will certainly be accomplished there.
Furthermore, there are superior locations spoken of by the Buddhas;
additionally, there are superior locations spoken of by Bodhisattvas, namely the sites of the eight great stūpas.
Or, there are famous mountains with many forests, abundant in fruits and where springs flow together—such places are described as superior locations.
“Alternatively, an araṇya that abounds in flowers and fruits and has flowing water that people delight in—such a place is called an excellent location.

Furthermore, an araṇya where there are many deer and no one hunts them, and which is free from beasts such as brown bears, black bears, tigers, and wolves—such a place is called an excellent location.”
"Where there is neither excessive cold nor excessive heat, and which is pleasant and agreeable to the mind—such a place is called a 'superior location' (śubha-sthāna).
It may be at the side of a mountain;
or it may be on a mountain peak."
Alternatively, there may be a solitary high terrace;
or on a mountainside where there is water—such places are described as excellent locations.

Furthermore, there are excellent locations where green grass covers the ground and many flowering trees abound, and among them are trees suitable for performing *homa*—such places are described as excellent locations.
"Either before a stūpa where the śarīra are enshrined;
or at a place in the mountains where the śarīra are enshrined;
or beside the four rivers;"
Or there may be an araṇya adorned with various kinds of trees where few people dwell;
or a cremation ground where smoke never ceases;
or the bank of a great river.
Or at a place where many cattle once resided;
or beneath a solitary great tree that is the abode of spirits and where the sun's shadow does not turn;
or at all the sacrificial sites of many villages.
"Alternatively, at the side of a crossroads,
or by the edge of a dragon pond— such places are called superior locations.
Or in whatever country the Buddha has traveled for walking meditation— in such directions, one will swiftly attain accomplishment."
"In any land where the populace has deep faith in the Triple Gem and propagates the True Dharma, such a place shall swiftly attain accomplishment.
Furthermore, in any land where there are many people endowed with compassion, such a place shall likewise swiftly attain accomplishment."

"Once such a supreme and wondrous location has been obtained, one must carefully select the site by removing impurities, shards, stones, and other such objects; this is explained in detail in each section of the Maṇḍala chapter. Furthermore, according to the rules for *siddhi*, one must properly distinguish the locations for the three families."

Furthermore, one must distinguish between the *śāntika* (pacifying), *pauṣṭika* (augmenting), and *ābhicāruka* (subjugating) rites; these three types of rites must also be distinguished as superior, middling, and inferior.

Alternatively, at that very spot, one should perform tasks such as smearing, sprinkling, and sweeping according to the mind’s disposition; thus, the methods for attaining *siddhi* will be swiftly accomplished. Chapter Seven:

The Classification of the Rules of Discipline (*Śīla-dharma-vibhāga*) from the Susiddhikara Sūtra. "Furthermore, I shall explain in detail the rules for establishing the precepts and maintaining the mantras. If one relies upon these precepts, one shall attain accomplishment before long."
If a wise person maintains various mantras, they should first sever all anger, such that they do not give rise to resentment even toward deities;
furthermore, they should harbor no anger toward other mantra-holders.
Regarding mantras, one should not arbitrarily interpret their efficacy or various ritual rules; rather, one should cultivate deep reverence for all mantras and their prescribed methods.
Furthermore, one must carefully protect against malicious persons. Why is this?

Because it can obstruct great matters and destroy them, one should not give rise to thoughts of arrogance toward the ācārya through the three karmas of body and so forth, even if one perceives faults in him; nor should one speak of various right and wrong with the mouth, nor ever harbor thoughts of discriminating faults in the mind. If this is so even regarding actual faults, how much more so when acting in accordance with the Dharma?

Even if one harbors great anger, one must ultimately not bind other vidyārājas with the mantras one holds oneself, nor inflict harm or punitive suffering upon them, nor should one perform rites for subduing enemies.
One should not grant the transmission of mantras to those who have never received them from an ācārya;

nor should one grant them to those who harbor no reverence for the Three Jewels or who belong to non-Buddhist paths (tīrthika). Even if such individuals have received mantras from an ācārya, they must not be given [the teachings]. Furthermore, neither the mudrās, nor the mantras, nor the methods of efficacy, nor the universal practices (sāmānyavidhi) shall be bestowed upon them.
Nor shall they be granted to those who have never previously entered a maṇḍala.
"One should not step over any two-legged sentient beings on the path, nor likewise those with many legs;
furthermore, one should not step over various terrestrial emblems, namely:
the mallet, the wheel, the vajra, the conch, the *bajra* [trident], and so forth, nor should one step over those made of cloth."
One should not discard other medicinal herbs— whether roots, stalks, branches, leaves, seeds, or fruits—
nor should one cast them into impure places.
"If one desires to accomplish the mantras of the Dharma, one should interrogate and debate the correct principles of the Mahāyāna."
If one hears of the profound, rare, and inconceivable conduct of a bodhisattva, one should give rise to sincere faith and harbor no doubts.
A mantra practitioner should not test another who also maintains the recitation;
nor, even on account of a minor transgression, should they employ rites of subjugation.

"One who delights in accomplishment should not sing or engage in playful banter with others; nor should they adorn their bodies by applying perfumes, ornaments, or wearing flower garlands, nor should they leap about.
One should not take pleasure in the body by floating playfully in rivers, and one should refrain from all forms of frivolous joking and laughter."
"There are three types of unwholesome karma that one must not commit, namely:
speaking falsehoods, speech arising from a defiled mind, and divisive speech, harsh words, and verbal abuse."
In responding to others, one should not rely on excessive words; one must never practice or engage in useless conversation.
Furthermore, one should not dwell together with non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*), nor speak with those of the *caṇḍāla* class who seek to challenge or provoke;
one should not converse with such people at all, except for one's own companions.
While reciting, one should not speak even to one's companions;
at other times of recitation, one should not speak to companions unless it is necessary;
nor should one smear oil upon the body.

Furthermore, one should not eat the five pungent roots, leeks, radishes, sesame seeds, nor any other leafy vegetables, rice flour, bean cakes, *māṣa* beans, or sesame cakes; nor should one eat food made into balls.
One must not consume any food favored by the *vināyakas*, nor food left over from offerings, nor sesame, non-glutinous rice, or bean porridge, nor milk porridge.

"Regarding all vehicles, if there is a specific cause or condition that permits riding them, one may do so; however, those that are not permitted, as well as those with saddles, must not be ridden at all.
This includes food that has been offered on the road or food that has been touched by others.
Furthermore, regarding all ornaments for the body, namely:"
One should not use mirrors, flowers, or powders and medicinal pastes as coverings; except for matters of necessity, one should not rub hand against hand or foot against foot.
One should not perform the acts of defecation or urination in or near any body of water.
One should not eat food supported by the hands alone, nor should one eat various leafy greens using copper vessels or hammers.
One must not turn over a vessel filled with food.
One should not lie down on large or small beds or couches;
one must not lie down together with another person.

When wishing to lie down, one should settle the mind in tranquility and lie down in purity; one should not lie face down nor lie on one's back, but rather lie on the right side like a lion king. While lying down, one must not sleep with eyes wide open.
"One should eat only one meal per day and not eat a second time;
one should not fast,
nor should one eat excessively."
One should not eat too much or too little; if there is any doubt regarding the food, one must not consume it.
One should avoid all frivolous play, large crowds, and even women; one must enter [the assembly] in such a manner and must not look at others.
One should not take pleasure in or become attached to dwellings or fine food that are pleasing to the body, speech, and mind;
one should accept poor dwellings and poor food, yet neither reject them nor abandon them.
One should not wear garments of purple, nor should one wear clothes that are old, torn, or soiled.
When performing recitation, one should wear undergarments and must not disparage oneself by saying,
"I have many transgressions and thus have no way to achieve siddhi.
Furthermore, one must not speak of the karma of previous lives.
Even if one suffers from physical swellings or various diseases that ultimately cause one to neglect the practice of recitation, one must never abandon the mantra received from the Ācārya.
Even if a voice should speak within a dream or from the sky, saying,
"You should not uphold this mantra-dharma," one must neither discard it nor feel anger toward that voice.
Why is this? Because they are all demons.

You must only apply yourself with diligence and not regress; do not harbor evil thoughts in your mind, do not pursue external objects, and do not let your sense faculties run wild. Constantly maintain purity and recite [the mantra].
"If one seeks great accomplishment, the mantra one personally maintains should not be used to subjugate demons or malevolent spirits;
nor should it be used to protect oneself or others;
nor should it be used for rescuing those in distress or restraining various poisons; furthermore, the mantra one maintains and all other mantras should not be employed for such purposes."
All mantras used according to their purpose should be recited with the *arbhimantra*; furthermore, one must not compete with others to test their efficacy.

If one desires to attain *siddhi*, one must perform the recitation during the three periods of the day; when performing purification, one should not use water alone, but rather wash with water consecrated by the mantra.
The mantra for holding and reciting over pure water is:
"Oṃ hūṃ haṃ va ra vajre ṇi ha. At the time of bathing, one should apply pure earth to the entire body for washing; this earth-mantra should be recited seven times over it.
The earth mantra is:

"Oṃ vara hāra hūṃ. Within the earth and water there are many obstacles and Vināyakas; one must first dispatch them before employing [the earth], reciting this mantra to drive them out from within the earth and water.
The mantra for dispelling obstacles is:
"Namaḥ varāya hūṃ haṃ khaṃ maṃtha vittaṃsāyuccharāya ṭhaḥ. Furthermore, first take water and stir it with the hand; once the mantra has been recited, use it.
The mantra for bathing is as follows: "Namaḥ ratnatrayāya."

*Namasyāya svāhā*. Recite this three times.
When bathing at will using water consecrated with this mantra, one should not engage in conversation.
Before the bathing is completed, one must mentally recite the following heart-mantra.
The heart-mantra for the time of bathing is:

"Oṃ amṛte hūṃ ṭhaḥ. Once the bathing is finished, one should take a handful of water with both hands, empower it seven times with the aforementioned heart-mantra, and pour it over the crown of the head.
In this manner, one should bind the top-knot three times, reciting the mantra seven additional times while forming the hair upon the crown of the head.
If one is a renunciant, one should form a fist with the right hand and place it upon the crown of the head, repeating the aforementioned number of recitations.
The mantra for binding the topknot is:

"Oṃ susiddhi kare svāhā. Next, one should wash the hands, take water, and rinse the mouth three times; thereafter, one should wash one's own deity, recite the root mantra seven times over the scripture, and recite the mouth-rinsing mantra over five places on the body.
The mantra is:

"Oṃ kili kili vajra hūṃ phaṭ. When the bathing is complete, visualize bathing the Honored One (the deity), and then at that spot, one should recite the mantra one maintains as many times as desired; thereafter, one may proceed to the usual place for recitation.

Until one has reached that destination, one should remain free from all unwholesome karma such as greed and delusion; with a single-minded purity, one should maintain a reverent visualization of the Honored One while proceeding slowly, strictly observing the prohibitions and precepts as previously established.
Having arrived at that place, one should immediately perform all ritual activities according to the Dharma and engage in recitation.
One should constantly maintain the site of the maṇḍala; when weary from recitation, one should read Mahāyāna sūtras or construct caityas, never neglecting or forgetting any other virtuous deeds.
One should take refuge in the Triple Gem at the three times of day;
repent of all remaining karmic offenses three times;
and generate the bodhicitta at the three times of day.
Make aspirations during the three periods of the day to accomplish these supreme matters; if you act in this way, you will swiftly attain accomplishment.

To eliminate transgressions, you should constantly fashion ten million images and stupas from fragrant clay, burn incense, scatter flowers, offer praise and worship, perform various virtuous deeds, practice constant giving, and be endowed with great compassion.

One should not give rise to stinginess regarding the teachings of all dharmas; one should always maintain patience and diligence, remain firm and non-regressive, and keep the six recollections in mind.

One should contemplate the meaning of the sūtras one hears, constantly recite the efficacy of mantras, always make offerings to the mantra-dharma-sūtras, and skillfully complete the wondrous maṇḍala according to the sūtras.
One must, in every thought-moment, give rise to the great bodhicitta; first, cause the bhikṣu-saṃgha to enter with true faith,
followed by the bhikṣuṇīs,
and then the upāsakas.
Next, the upāsikās entered in successive order, all of whom firmly resolved their minds toward bodhicitta and established a definitive right view.

Once they had completed their entry into the maṇḍala, one should bestow upon them the methods for binding hand-mudrās, mantras, and other dharmas of the Vidyā-piṭaka; furthermore, one should extensively proclaim all the rules for mantra practice.

Whether on the fourteenth day, or the eighth and the final day of the month, or on the eleventh and fifteenth days—on such days, one should redouble the offerings of incense, flowers, food, and all other requisites; furthermore, by performing recitation, *homa*, empowerments, and observing the precepts, and by constantly maintaining mindfulness and redoubling these various practices, the mantra will be accomplished.
"When performing the homa, one must always hold a vajra in hand and recite the mantra more than a thousand times.
The mantra of Karmavajrin for accomplishing activities is:
'Oṃ dhuna vajra ha. If one wishes to fashion a vajra for performing various ritual activities, one should use wood burnt by celestial fire or *kṛmika* wood."
One may take embers from a cremated corpse, charred wood, or red sandalwood;
taking any one of these woods, one should fashion a *vajra* provided with three prongs.
During the performance of *homa* and during recitation, one should always hold it with the right hand. Because it can accomplish all matters, it is called the "all-accomplishing *vajra*."
If one grasps [the ritual], all *vināyakas* and other obstructors will be terrified and flee in all directions.

Anoint a *vajra* with red sandalwood incense and place it before the principal deity; recite the prescribed mantra while making offerings of flowers and incense. Through this, all activities and other matters will be accomplished by the subtle and wondrous power of the Vajra Secret.

"When performing any rites, one must always keep the right arm and hand bound with a mantra-cord; holding the rosary-cord in the right hand and having the arm anointed with fragrant unguents, one should recite the mantra either one hundred or one thousand times."
The mantra of the Pāśa is:
"Oṃ kuraṇḍari bandha bandha hūṃ phaṭ. This Vidyārāja’s Great Seal is named Mañjuśrī; it can accomplish all Vidyārāja mantras, and can also augment and fulfill the words and phrases of mantras.
It can also accomplish all other ritual matters, including such things as the purification of the body; it is not only the mother of the Vidyārājas, but also the Mother of the Vajras.

"If for the Vajra family cord one uses the *mūlamantra* twice and further pierces the center of the cord to form a knot, following the method for making cords according to the Vajra family, it should be known that for the two [other] families, knots are made using lotus seeds and so forth;
for a cord of the Buddha family, one should employ the *mātṛ-mantra*;
if it is a cord of the Lotus family, one should employ the *bhañjaravāsini-mantra*, as previously stated."
One who wears and carries these cords will not be obstructed by vināyakas.
For the cord of the Buddha Family, one should employ the mantra of the Buddha-Mother; that mantra is named Buddhalocanā, and its mantra is as before.
If it is for the Lotus Family cord, one should employ Pañcarakṣā; her mantra is as before.

"Those who wear and carry these cords will not be obstructed by vināyakas; their bodies shall attain purity, they will swiftly achieve accomplishment, and all their sought-after wishes will be fulfilled."

Furthermore, when performing the rite, one should fashion a finger-ring from *kuśa* grass and place it upon the ring finger of the right hand; having recited either the three-and-a-half-syllable heart-mantra of the respective family one hundred or one thousand times, one should then fix it upon the finger.
The Heart Mantra of the Buddha Family is:
"Eṇa eka. The Heart Mantra of the Lotus Family is:
"Arolika. The Heart Mantra of the Vajra Family is: [as above].

“*Vajra-dṛka-laghu.* When performing offerings, reciting mantras, or conducting homa, one should wear a grass bracelet (*darbha-kaṅkaṇa*). By wearing this grass ring, karmic obstructions are eliminated, the hands become purified, and all undertakings are accomplished.”

Furthermore, take white cotton thread and hemp fibers, have a young girl dye them red or the color of saffron, and combine them to make thread. Take this to form a mantra-cord (*mantra-sūtra*), reciting the mantra seven times for each knot; thus, making one knot after another until there are seven knots. Place it before the deity and perform the recitation of the sutra one thousand times while maintaining the mantra.

When reciting mantras, performing homa, or when about to lie down to sleep, one should fasten it around the waist; for when sleeping at night, it is necessary to wear a girdle so as not to lose seminal impurity.

The mantra for holding the cord is: “Oṃ hara hara bandha bandha kṣetrāṇi siddhārāja svāhā. When reciting this or performing homa, one must wear the lower garment and drape the upper robe over the right shoulder. However, this rule does not apply when lying down, washing, or bathing; the upper garment worn at those times need not be consecrated with the mantra.
When defecating or urinating, one should wear wooden sandals; however, one must not wear them before the deity, before the upādhyāya or ācārya, or before other venerable elders.
Regarding those objects of attachment, one should make offerings with body, speech, and mind to the various venerable ones.
"If one desires that siddhi be swiftly attained, one should always pay homage to caityas and bhikṣus;
however, if one encounters the images of external deities, one should merely join the palms or recite gāthās."
If one sees a venerable one, one should likewise pay them homage;
if one hears the sublime Dharma, one should give rise to deep reverence and faith;
and if one hears of the inconceivable deeds of Bodhisattvas, or the various accomplishments achieved through mantras, one should in every case rejoice with a heart full of exultation.
If you wish to achieve success swiftly, you should always be diligent and never give rise to indolence.

You must constantly reflect upon the precepts as previously established; if you do not act accordingly, you will violate the prohibitive precepts, incur grave offenses, and siddhi will not be attained.

"One must constantly guard and mind the physical body and all the sense faculties, refraining from craving or attachment; furthermore, one should always practice as previously prescribed without neglect or forgetfulness.
If one commits various evil deeds during the morning hours, one should perform repentance by evening;
if one commits various evil deeds during the night, one should sincerely repent by morning."

Furthermore, one must maintain pure recitation of mantras and attend to all other matters; as prescribed by the fundamental precepts, one should act accordingly and not allow time to pass in vain. One must constantly apply the mind to the precepts of the Vidyārāja, for only then will one dwell soon in *siddhi*.
Chapter Eight: The Chapter on Offering Flowers from the Susiddhikara Sūtra. "Furthermore, the three categories of rites shall be explained in detail.
These three categories consist of the śāntika (pacifying) rite, the pauṣṭika (prosperity) rite, and the ābhicāruka (subjugating/terrible) rite, along with all other such rites."
Each of the three families has three grades of mantras, namely:
those spoken by the Noble Ones, those spoken by the devas, and those spoken by the earth-dwelling devas.
These constitute the three families.
The "Noble" refers to those who speak—namely Buddhas, Bodhisattvas, Śrāvakas, and Pratyekabuddhas; these are the mantras of the Noble Ones.
The "Devas" refers to those who speak, from the Śuddhāvāsa Heavens down to the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven; these are the mantras of the Devas.

Regarding those spoken by the earth-dwelling devas: that which is spoken by yakṣas, rākṣasas, asuras, nāgas, garuḍas, gandharvas, kiṃnaras, mahoragas, bhūtas, piśācas, kumbhāṇḍas, and so forth, constitutes the mantras of the earth-dwelling devas.
"If one performs the śāntika rite, one should employ the mantras of the Noble Ones;
if one performs the pauṣṭika rite, one should employ the mantras of the devas;
if one performs the ābhicāruka rite, one should employ the mantras of the earth-dwelling deities (bhaumadevatās)."
If one seeks the highest accomplishment, one should employ the mantras of the Noble Ones;
if one seeks middling accomplishment, one should employ the mantras of the devas;
if one seeks inferior accomplishment, one should employ the mantras of the earth-dwelling spirits (bhūmideva).
Thus, each of the three families has three grades of accomplishment.

When performing these three types of rites, one should equally employ various colored flowers grown both in water and on land. Distinguishing them according to their names and colors based on their respective families, one should offer these mantra-flowers while making this aspiration:
"These flowers are pure, and their place of origin is likewise pure; I now offer them, praying that you will graciously accept them and grant me accomplishment."
The mantra for offering flowers is:
"Oṃ ahara ahara sarvabhūtaya dhāra pūrti svāhā. Using this mantra, one should consecrate the flowers and offer them to the three families.
If one offers flowers to the Buddha, one should use white flowers and fragrances to make the offering;
if one offers to Avalokiteśvara, one should use white flowers grown in water to make the offering;
if one offers to Vajrapāṇi, one should use various kinds of incense and flowers to make the offering.
If one makes offerings to the terrestrial deities, one should offer various flowers gathered according to the season.

The flowers that should be offered are: the *mālatī*, the *pāṭala*, the lotus, the *campaka*, the *nāgarāja*, the *yūthikā*, the *kunduru*, the *vārṣika* and *mallikā*, the *jātī*, the *phalgu*, the *kruvaka*, the *kadamba*, the *mṛdunika*, the *kairava*, the *vātāpuṣpa*, the *bhaṇḍīra*, the *navamālikā*, the *arjaka*, the *mucukunda*, the *nāgakesara*, and the *cūtamañjarī*.
All nine types [of flowers] may be used interchangeably; one need not restrict oneself to specific flowers.
If, when performing the rite, the prescribed flowers cannot be obtained, one may offer whatever flowers are available.
When making offerings with flowers, one should use the flower-mantra of the specific family (*kula*) to which they belong.

If there are no flowers for offering, one should use the three branches and leaves of the *surasa*, or the *māluṅga* flower, the leaves of the *tanduna*, the leaves of the *dambara*, the leaves of the *kṛṣṇamallikā*, the leaves of the *mandūkaparṇī*, the leaves of the *elārajaka*, as well as the leaves of the *lāṅgalī* and so forth, to present as an offering.

"If these branches and leaves are unavailable, one should instead use the roots of *vālaka*, spikenard (*uśīra*), *selaginella* and *achyranthes*, as well as the roots of various fragrant medicinal herbs and the roots of fragrant fruits; these may also be used for offering."
That is to say, cloves, cardamom, nutmeg, raisins, and various fragrant fruits are also suitable for offering alongside flowers as an act of worship.

"If one does not have the flowers, leaves, roots, or fruits mentioned above for offering, it has been heard that one may offer flowers, or if one has previously offered flowers oneself, one should perform a visualization of making offerings according to what is appropriate; this is the most supreme and excellent offering to the Honored Dharma."

"Even though one may offer flowers, fruits, and so forth as previously described, if one can, with a sincere heart and reverent devotion, join the palms and offer flowers and fruits to the head of the Honored One (Bhagavān), such mental worship is supreme and unsurpassed. One should always perform such offerings without harboring doubt, and then accomplishment will be attained."
