Śṛṅgavera-sarja-rasa,
bābhi, kīśalaya, and other such substances, as well as resinous extracts; namely:

Karpūra (camphor), yantarasāsa, carasa, agallochum, frankincense, śalākīśa, vāsasapuṣpa, mukula-aindrīpuṣpa, karka-rapuṣpa, caitrarathapuṣpa, bhaṇijñāpuṣpa, utpalapuṣpa, dākarapuṣpa, kuṇḍanapuṣpa, and karabhapuṣpa—these and others, which grow in forest hermitages and in both water and on land in the region of Lin-yi, such as these, one should properly know how to employ according to the three families and three grades for flower offerings.
"Using *mālatī* flowers, *tagara* flowers, *kundana* flowers, *mallikā* flowers, *yūthikā* flowers, and *nāgapuṣpa* flowers—such flowers as these are for offering to the Buddha Family (*buddhakula*).

Using *utpala* flowers, *kumuda* flowers, lotuses, *pārijātaka* flowers, *śephālikā* flowers, *campaka* flowers, and *tagara* flowers—such flowers as these are supreme for making offerings within the Avalokiteśvara Family (*padmakula*).
Using blue lotuses, *pāṭalī* flowers, leaves, branches, twigs, and others not specifically mentioned, one should offer them throughout the Vajra Family (*vajrakula*)."
"As with the flowers mentioned above, those that are white are for performing the *śāntika* rite;
those that are yellow are for performing the *pauṣṭika* rite;
and those that are purple are for performing the *abhicāruka* rite."
"Thus, among these flowers, those with a sweet taste are used for *śāntika* rites;
those with a pungent taste are used for *abhicāruka* rites;
and those with a bland taste are used for *pauṣṭika* rites."
There are branches and flowers produced in pure places;
there are sprouts of young *māḍa* grass or small herbaceous flowers;
and there are flowers of medium-sized trees and large trees.
Various kinds of flowers should be used according to their respective types.
Specifically, the *kumuda* (dark-colored) flower is to be offered exclusively to the Buddha;
if it is a red lotus, it is to be offered exclusively to Avalokiteśvara.
If blue lotuses are offered exclusively to Vajra,
each is said to be supreme.
Within the Buddha Family, when performing the śāntika rite, one uses *añjani-sumana* flowers.
For the performance of the pauṣṭika rite, use red lotuses;
for the performance of the ābhicāruka rite, use blue lotuses.
In the remaining two categories, act accordingly in this manner.

"Superior-colored fragrant flowers and inferior-colored fragrant flowers are to be used according to the specific rite; whether using flower stalks or fallen blossoms to offer to the Queen of Heaven (Devī) is said to be most excellent.
Purple and white *karamara* flowers, when offered to the Wrathful Lord (Krodheśvara) and his messengers, are said to be most excellent.

As for *khajūra*, *tilaka*, *bala*, *kalikāra*, *asana-ruma*, *vīra*, and *kaṭhara* flowers, one should take whichever is available and recite the mantra once for each to perform offerings that penetrate the three obstructions, as well as the three [rites] for the removal of calamities—superior, middling, and inferior."
Furthermore, one may fashion garlands by combining various kinds of flowers, or offer them as a collection of diverse blossoms.

Among the nine general types of flowers, only those that emit a foul odor, grow on thorny trees, or possess a bitter or acrid taste are unfit for offering; likewise, those not previously listed by name in the extensive enumeration should not be used.
Additionally, flowers with wooden stems, *ketakī* flowers, *adhimuktaka* flowers, *māndārava* flowers, and *campaka* flowers are also unsuitable for use.
"Regarding the ninefold long-term offerings:

red flowers, *kuṃsumā* flowers, *pālaṅgu* flowers, *kharjūra* grass and the like, as well as rice blossoms, mixed with sesame seeds for offering—these various flowers and so forth mentioned above are the most supreme for making offerings."

If such flowers for offering are unavailable, one may instead use white non-glutinous rice, carefully selecting and discarding the broken grains, as well as *ka* and other fragrant resins from trees containing sap; these should all be properly blended according to their respective families (*kula*).
"Mix various grasses, fragrant roots, juices, incense, flowers, and so forth—these three types of substances—together to form an unguent for offering to the Buddha Family.

Furthermore, take the bark of various fragrant trees, white sandalwood, aloeswood, and celestial wood, along with the aforementioned types of incense and fragrant fruits; combine these as previously distinguished to form an unguent for use by the Lotus Family.
Again, combine various fragrant herbs, roots, flowers, fruits, leaves, and so forth to form an unguent for use by the Vajra Family."

Alternatively, there may be unguents composed of various roots and fruits, or those whose fragrance was blended by former masters and is particularly superior; these also pertain to the three families.
"Or one may use only aloeswood incense mixed with a small amount of camphor as an unguent for offerings to the Buddha Family;
or one may use only white sandalwood incense mixed with a small amount of camphor as an unguent for use in the Lotus Family."

Alternatively, one may use saffron mixed with a small amount of camphor as an unguent for use in the Vajra Family; furthermore, red sandalwood may be used as an unguent, which is applicable to all [families], including the Vajra and others.

"Use *kakkola*, *caraṇābjaraja*, *sumana*, or *śrīkhaṇḍa* mixed with honey and clarified butter, as well as *śvetarocanā* and so forth, as unguents to offer to all the messenger deities (*dūtadevatā*).
Furthermore, use *tagara* and *śrīkhaṇḍa* mixed with *kakkola* as unguents to offer to the queens of the Vidyārājas.
Moreover, use white sandalwood, *agaru*, and *kuṅkuma* as unguents to offer to the Vidyārājas."
Furthermore, the bark of various fragrant trees is used as unguent to offer to the messengers;
additionally, whatever fragrance is available may be used as unguent to offer to the earth-dwelling devas.
Alternatively, agarwood alone may be used as unguent, applicable in all instances for the three families, the ninefold dharma cycles, and for the queens of the vidyā-rājas.
"If one performs a *śāntika* rite, one should use white incense;
if a *pauṣṭika* rite, yellow incense;
and if an *abhicāruka* rite, purple incense that is odorless."
"If one wishes to achieve the great *siddhi*, one should use the aforementioned liquid incense along with fragrant fruits;
if one wishes to achieve the middling *siddhi*, one should use hard-wood incense and flowers;
if one wishes to achieve the lesser *siddhi*, one should use root, bark, incense, flowers, and fruits as unguents for worship."
"One should not apply blended fragrant substances to the body of a sentient being;

that is to say, substances such as musk, *cīnaka*, and other perfumes, as well as wine, vinegar, or those used in excess, are not to be employed for making offerings as they are not fit for worldly use."
"Furthermore, there are four kinds of incense:
namely, ointment incense, powdered incense, granular incense, and pill incense."
Using whichever incense is available, one should offer it throughout the entire altar as flowers, making offerings daily.
When wishing to present them, one should make this vow:
"This incense is fragrant like the wondrous incense of the heavens; may it be pure and provide protection. I now offer it to you; please graciously accept it and cause my vows to be fulfilled."
The mantra for the scented ointment is:

“Aghora aghora (1) sarva-bhūti-ya-dara (2) pūrṇa svāhā (3). Recite this mantra over the scented ointment, then recite your own personal mantra and, having purified it according to the ritual rules, offer it to the Honored One.

If one seeks various incenses but cannot obtain them, one should take any available unguent and recite the mantra over it; then, using the specific unguent mantra of one's own family, one should offer the incense to the principal deity.

10. Chapter on the Classification of Incense Burning. *Susiddhikara Sūtra*, Chapter Ten: The Classification of Incense Burning. "Furthermore, I shall now explain the methods for burning incense belonging to the three families."
That is to say:

agarwood, white sandalwood, saffron, and so forth; one should take these for offering according to their respective order, or combine three types of incense to correspond with the three families, or take a single type of incense to correspond with one's own family.
The names of the incenses listed are:

śrīveṣṭaka, khaḍiraja-sarjarasa, rocanā-gandharasa, guggulu, sarjarasa, karpūra, turuṣka, vṛkadhūpa, girija-madhu, harītakī, granthika, kuṅkuma, agaru, spṛkkā, candana, tamālapattra, pañcapatra, devadāru, nālikerāmbu, kapilāva-usīra, śarkarā, vacā, and fragrant fruits.

"If one wishes to accomplish the mantra rites of the three families, one should compound incense: *śrīveṣṭaka* resin incense is universally applicable to all three families and suitable for offerings to all devas;
*guggulu* incense is suitable for offerings to yakṣas;
and *kunduruka* incense is suitable for offerings to all devas and devīs."
Offer *saccharasa* incense to the earth-dwelling devas;
offer *salākī* incense to the female messengers;
offer *gandharasa* incense to the male messengers.

“Karpūra, gandhasāra, sarjarasa, kunduruka, guggulu, sallakī, and śrīvāsaka—these seven resinous incenses (gavya-gandha) are blended together and burned; they pervade all nine types [of incense], and these seven incenses are said to be the most supreme.”
Resin incense is superior;
hard-wood incense is middling;
other flowers, leaves, roots, and so forth are inferior.
"Sugandha, agallochum, saffron, and other such incenses blended together constitute the first [type of] incense;
adding white sandalwood and granulated sugar constitutes the second incense;
and adding guggulu and frankincense constitutes the third incense."
These three types of blended incense may each be used individually for all general purposes;
furthermore, for the terrestrial devas and their protectors, one should use *sajjara-sā* (resin), granulated sugar, and *harītakī*, blending them as incense to make offerings to them.
"Furthermore, there are five fragrant substances, namely:
granulated sugar, śrīveṣṭaka, saptaparṇa, harītakī, and rock honey; when blended together, they form an incense that is applicable to all ritual functions of the three families."
There may be a single fragrance that universally applies to all matters, such as a superior incense esteemed by all people—a wondrously blended incense.
If such a fragrance is not available, one may use whatever is at hand, which likewise applies to the various ritual functions of the three families.

Regarding the methods for compounding incense as described above, one must skillfully distinguish these incense formulas; when it is time to offer them, one should do so by combining the appropriate roots, leaves, flowers, and fruits.
Furthermore, there are four kinds of incense that must be known:
namely, natural incense, stick-incense, coarse-powder incense, and pellet-incense; one must also know the appropriate applications for each.
"If for the *śāntika* rite, one uses incense in the form of pellets;
if for the *abhicāruka* rite, one uses powdered incense;
and if for the *pauṣṭika* rite, one uses incense made into pills."

"To encompass all applications, one should combine the self-nature incense with powdered incense and resin incense, using granulated sugar; for the pellet incense, it should be blended with high-quality honey;
or else, the incense may be mixed with clarified butter, milk, granulated sugar, and honey."

One should place a small amount of clarified butter upon the natural incense; then, using the incense prescribed for burning in the specific family (*kula*) one seeks, or if that is unavailable, any available incense, first universally apply it to the respective family by reciting the incense mantra and spell of that family, and thereafter recite the mantra one maintains while performing the method for blending the incense.

One should not place on it scents such as *nakha*, musk, or *candana*; nor should one employ substances such as *manjika*. Furthermore, blended fragrances must not be excessive, lest they result in a foul odor rather than a pleasant scent.

"By means of these fragrances from the trees and forests of this grove, and this resinous incense, which can transform the aspirations of all people and are constantly consumed by the devas, I now offer them; may you look upon me with compassion and graciously accept them."
The Incense Mantra:

"Aghora aghora sarva-bhūtebhyo dhara pūrṇa svāhā. One must recite this mantra while consecrating the incense; one should recite the specific mantra of the deity being worshipped, for the incense is offered according to the ritual rules.

Chapter Eleven: The Ritual for Lighting Lamps from the Susiddhikara Sūtra Furthermore, I shall now explain the three types of rituals for lighting lamps; by performing them according to the Dharma, one causes the celestial beings and sages to rejoice and brings about accomplishment.
Whether made of gold, silver, refined copper, or of porcelain or earthenware—among these five types, whichever is used in accordance with the Dharma will bring joy to the tutelary deity.
To make the wick of a lamp, one may use white cotton flowers;
or use new cotton cloth;
or use the fibers from the bark of the *nuguḷa* tree.
Alternatively, one may employ newly purified cloth.
Use superior fragrant oils that are pleasing to many,
or various types of incense-infused ghee and oil.
For the śāntika rite, use superior fragrant oil;
for the pauṣṭika rite, use intermediate fragrant oil;
for the ābhicāruka rite, use inferior fragrant oil.
"If fragrant wood oil is used for *śāntika*;
if sesame oil is used for *pauṣṭika*;
if white mustard seed oil is used for *abhicāruka*."
The *āmalaka* fruit oil is used by the Mantra Consorts, the Queen of the Later [Period], and the various female seers (*ṛṣikanyā*);
if it is fruit oil from other fruits, it is used by the Mantra Lords;
if it is fruit oil from trees, it is used by the devas and the māhakāras.
If fish fat is used, it is for making offerings to the *bhūtas*;
if the fat of various domestic animals is used, it is for making offerings to the *yakṣas*;
if *bhallātaka* oil or sesame oil is used, it is for making offerings to the lower classes of devas, as well as for the Four Sisters, the *Cāmuṇḍās*, and so forth.
If a vetāla arises in a cemetery, use large quantities of meat and fat.
Among all oils, buffalo ghee is supreme for the three families.
Furthermore, white cow ghee is used for śāntika rites;
The ghee of a yellow bull is used for pauṣṭika;
the ghee of a black bull is used for ābhicāruka.
If there are specific distinctions within one's own family (kula), one should also use them according to those [distinctions].
"Oil produced from medicinal herbs is used for pauṣṭika;
oil produced from fragrant substances is used for śāntika;
and oil with a foul odor is used for ābhicāruka."

"As briefly explained above regarding the ritual procedures for the lamp, one should carefully observe them oneself; even if these have not been mentioned here, they should be applied with due scrutiny. Although there may be lamp oil that does not belong to a specific division, it is also permissible to offer it after consecrating it with the mantra of one's own primary division."
"The lamp can dispel obstructions and burn away the darkness; I now offer this to you—may you accept it out of compassion.
The Lamp Mantra:

"Oṃ aruṇaya aruṇaya sarvabuddhadharmapūjite svāhā. Having recited this mantra, one next recites the root-holding mantra (*mūladhāraṇī*) and consecrates [the offering]. Furthermore, because one must perform the purification rite to eliminate all faults, one should practice according to the instructions given in the previous chapter.

12. Chapter on the Offering of Food. *Susiddhikara Sūtra*, Chapter Twelve: The Offering of Food. "Furthermore, I shall now explain the method for offering food, so that all celestial beings (devas) may be fully delighted and [the practitioner] may swiftly attain accomplishment."
To summarize the offering of food:
one should use round roots, long roots, and various fruits;
as well as cakes made with ghee and cakes made with oil.
Various soups and stews;
or various types of congees and other foods and drinks.
These four kinds of food may be offered universally to all the families.
The fruit of the *moraṭa* tree is common to all three families;
furthermore, the pomegranate fruit and the *juna* fruit are likewise common to all three families.
To indicate their respective order, each is assigned to one specific family.
If the taste is sweet, it is used for *śāntika* rites;
if the taste is sweet and sour, it is used for *pauṣṭika* rites;
if the taste is pungent or bland, it is used for *abhicāruka* rites.

"If there are fruits of the tāla tree, fruits of the yajñā fruit, fruits of the bilva, fruits of the nīpa, or other foul-smelling fruits that are not pleasing to the assembly, one should not offer them."
"There may be fruits of superior flavor that are abundant in the world and most precious; by offering such fruits, one attains the supreme accomplishment (*uttamasiddhi*).

There may be various fruits whose flavor is moderately delicious, which are easily obtained in the world and are not particularly valuable in price; by offering such fruits, one attains the middling accomplishment (*madhyamasiddhi*).

There may be various fruits whose flavor is bitter, pungent, bland, or the like, which are plentiful in the world and most inexpensive in price; by offering such fruits, one attains the inferior accomplishment (*adhamasiddhi*)."
"If one wishes to make offerings with focused intent, one should take the names of female deities;
that is to say, fruits such as persimmons, apricots, and peaches should be offered to the Goddesses;
and all tree-grown fruits that lack a bitter taste should be offered to the Consorts of the Mantras."
The śrīphala fruit may be offered to all three families;
the karkandhu fruit is offered exclusively to all yakṣas;
and the kapittha fruit is offered to Śrīdevī.
One should offer the fruit produced by the *paryaṅka* tree to Pāñcika.
There are many other such fruits with various alternative names; one should offer whichever is appropriate after observing its flavor.
"Alternatively, if there are sweet-tasting roots of various plants by a village or in a pure place such as an araṇya, one may take them and offer them, and success will likewise be attained."
The *ciṅgalī* root is suitable for all ritual applications;
furthermore, its extraordinary and delicious flowers, roots, stems, and leaves may also be offered, as they are used not only by celestial deities but also among humans.
"Those roots that grow in the mountains which possess a delicious flavor are for offering to the Buddha Family; furthermore, cooked yam roots are also suitable for the Buddha Family.
Moreover, the roots of the *kācilindika*, the *ciñcālikā*, the *kubjaka*, and other round roots, as well as those produced in water, are used for the Lotus Family.
Furthermore, all medicinal round roots that are bitter, pungent, or bland, and various kinds of raw yams, are used for the Vajra Family."
"Furthermore, those with round roots that are white in color, fragrant, and extremely sweet in taste are for offering to the Buddha Family;
those with round roots that are yellow in color, fragrant, and neither too sour nor too sweet in taste are for use in the Lotus Family;
and those with round roots that are red in color, fragrant, bitter, pungent, or faintly malodorous and not sweet in taste are for use in the Vajra Family."
Thus, the *śāntika* rites and other methods of these three families, as well as their superior, middling, and inferior [practices], are all to be used in common.

To speak briefly, one should properly accord with each family according to its superior, middling, or inferior [grade] and offer them accordingly; by making such distinctions, one will swiftly attain accomplishment.

These include round roots and long roots, as well as their growth and applications according to their respective categories; likewise, onions, garlic, scallions, leeks, and extremely foul-smelling, bitter, or acrid substances such as *piṅgu* and *tūda* should not be used for offerings.
"Śaṣṭika rice, urubhika cakes, pupa cakes, vaṇaka cakes, and other flour-based foods; or various kinds of sesame balls;
or various kinds of white sugar confections, modakas, maṇḍuśikas, piṇḍakas, bhaṅginna-koṭakas, aśoka-vatsyāyanas, and dāna..."
Food from Śrāvastī, food consisting of cakes, food consisting of *arapiṣṭaka*, food consisting of *śaṅkucita*,
food consisting of *pūpa*, food consisting of *prāṇa*, food consisting of *maṃsabhūpa*, food consisting of *ciñcāṭaka*,
food consisting of *puṣpavarta*, food consisting of *lāvaṇika*, and food consisting of *arkapuṣpaka*.
...Kukujñāna-bhakṣa, Rāmaṅga-bhakṣa, Khaṅsa-bhakṣa,
Siktika-bhakṣa, Pṛthak-cihlika-bhakṣa, Śrīphulaka-bhakṣa, Vaiśeṣika-bhakṣa, Cchinnaka-bhakṣa,
Chinnaraka-bhakṣa, Guṇapura-bhakṣa, Jñāti-... [bhakṣa].
Namely: *lābu-puṣpa* food, *kharjūra* food, *uḍumbara-pātala-śrīphalaka* food,
*kataka* food, various *arkacchinna-puṣpa* foods,
*rājāṃśa* food, *sāyaka* food, *kṛtāpūlaka* food, and *kāmuka* food.
Food, *kusārikā* food, *śakunāhāra* food, *miśrapuṭa* food,
*śaṇava* food, *harītakī* food, various *pralambha-riṣṭaka* foods,
*dibika* food, *jalahasitiniyama* food, *karkara* food, and so forth.
The food of Piṇḍaka, the food of Varāgada, the food of Vartimika,
the food of Ṭakṣaka, the food of Karkarṇika, and so forth.
As mentioned above, these may be made using granulated sugar, or with ghee,
or by mixing with sesame oil.
If one employs [the ritual] according to its own family and follows the dharma, making offerings in accordance with the rite, one will swiftly attain accomplishment.
If one uses rice-flour food, it is for the Buddha Family to perform śāntika and the highest accomplishment;
if one uses all types of grain-flour food, it is for the Lotus Family to perform pauṣṭika and the middling accomplishment.
If one consumes sesame seeds or beans, they are used for the *abhicāruka* rites and inferior accomplishments within the Vajra Family.
Among all flavors of food, those adorned with white sugar should always be offered within the Buddha Family;
if it is *śrīveṣṭaka* food, it is used for the Lotus Family.
If it is a *modaka* (joy-balls), it is for use by the Vajra Family;
if it is *pūpa* (cakes), it is for use by the Yakṣas;
if it is a "woman-named" food, it is for use by the Mantra Queens (*vidyārājñī*).
Regarding the names of the female deities who consume [the offerings]:

they are Kṣemalībhakṣī and Pāpabhakṣī; these are the most exquisite among all foods. One should offer them when seeking supreme accomplishment (*uttamasiddhi*). As for the remaining two families, one uses the next best flavors; those not included herein are used according to the food available for the eight classes of beings and others.
"At the time of making the food offering, first spread out cloths and fruit leaves as an adornment.

First place the *sāṣṭika* rice, the *lūbika* rice, and the *pūpa* cakes; thus, first perform the offerings common to the three families. Furthermore, according to what is required by one's own specific family (*kula*), offer whatever food and drink you can afford—namely, non-glutinous rice, sixty-day ripening non-glutinous rice, barley milk-rice, non-sown self-growing non-glutinous rice, and millet rice. Whatever is to be offered, offer it according to the ritual procedure, along with various fragrant and exquisite soups and stews, as well as various bean-based stews."
"One seeks the supreme accomplishment through milk-boiled barley rice and uncultivated, self-grown non-glutinous rice;
one seeks the middling accomplishment through ordinary non-glutinous rice and its cooked rice, or sixty-day-matured non-glutinous rice;
and one seeks the inferior accomplishment through millet and its cooked rice."
"The *śāntika* rite is for supreme accomplishment;
with millet and rice, one seeks inferior accomplishment—the *śāntika* rite is for supreme accomplishment, while with millet and rice, one seeks inferior accomplishment."
"The Śāntika rite is the supreme accomplishment;
the Pauṣṭika rite is the middling accomplishment;
and the Ābhicāruka rite is the inferior accomplishment."
"One should offer food and drink, roots and fruits, and rice porridge, presenting them according to the categories of superior, middling, and inferior.
For the *śāntika* rite, the superior belongs to the Buddha Family;
for the *pauṣṭika* rite, the middling belongs to the Lotus Family."
Regarding the *ābhicāruka* rites: the lower [attainments] belong to the Vajra Family.
One should understand that for the highest, middle, and lower *siddhis*, one must properly follow the ritual according to their respective categories.
"Among the flavors of soups and stews, those that are sweet are used for *śāntika* rites;
those that are sour-sweet are used for *pauṣṭika* rites;
and those that are bitter, pungent, or bland are used for *abhicāruka* rites."
"Milk gruel is for use in *śāntika* rites;
pomegranate gruel, curd gruel, and so forth are for use in *pauṣṭika* rites;
as for *kṣāra* gruel, it means: "
Sesame, non-glutinous rice, beans, and so forth are used for *abhicāruka* rites.

As previously stated regarding the various flavors of food and so on, or according to the diverse differences found in various regions, one should offer them after discerning their superior, middling, or inferior qualities;
or whatever flavors are praised by the multitude, or those which one personally loves, should be held and offered to the Buddha.
Alternatively, one should follow the sequence for offering food as taught in the mantra of one’s own specific family (*kula*); if it differs from that, accomplishment will not be attained.

Regarding the food, those that are prominent and those with foul odors are for use in the Vajra Family; as previously stated, the ointments, incense, lamps, and food each follow their respective families, while the *śāntika* and other rites follow their specific chapters. One should contemplate the nature of the mantra to determine whether it is joyful or wrathful.
"Next, one should further contemplate: 'What kind of matter is accomplished by this?
Furthermore, upon close investigation, what aspirations are fulfilled?
Having observed and understood this, one should offer the previously presented food according to one's capacity."

"In the ritual of offering, if one observes the use of *kāmika* food, one should offer *sāṣṭika* rice, *ulumbikā* food, and whatever other foods are available according to one's means, such as sugar, curd-rice, roots, fruits, milk-porridge, and so forth."
This *kāmika* food may be offered universally to all [deities], with the sole exception of those for whom *ābhicāruka* rites are performed.
Regarding the ritual procedures for making offerings, if one observes that *ciñcā-ḍola* food is required, one should add two or three varieties of superior, extraordinary foods to the *kāmika* food.
"If one sees the offering ritual involving *kṛsarā*, it means that one should place double the amount of the previously mentioned *kāmbika* food therein.
If one sees the offering ritual involving the 'three white foods,' these should be milk, curd, and ghee with rice;
furthermore, if one sees the 'three sweet foods,' these are ghee, honey, and milk-rice."

"If, within the ritual of offering, one sees *sarvabhojya* food, *sāyaliya* food, *laṅgaliya* food, *campriya* food, or *tilapiṣṭaka* food, as well as curd-rice, roots, and fruits—taking any one or two flavors from among these aforementioned foods and placing them upon rice-grain flowers, various flowers, and leaves; then filling a large vessel with water and placing [the food] therein—one should carry it far away from the place of recitation and discard it."

"If, within the ritual of offering, one sees the *śāntika* food, one should employ *sāstī* milk, congee, rice blossoms, ghee, honey, milk, and porridge made from parched barley, as well as foods such as *ciñcāphala*; one will certainly eliminate calamities, so have no doubt."

"If one observes the presence of *puṣṭika* (nourishing) food within the ritual of offering, one should employ such foods as curd-rice, curd-gruel, *modaka* (joy-balls), *ulūpikā*, sugar, and *śrīveṣṭaka*; one will certainly fulfill one's wishes—of this there is no doubt."

"If, within the ritual of offering, one sees the *abhicāruka* food, one should employ red non-glutinous rice, or *kudraka* seeds, or rice dyed red, or sesame cakes, *saphoṭaka*, *jambūliya*, *kṣāra*-gruel, and so forth; it will certainly subdue the māras without doubt."
"If one holds the mantras of yakṣas but lacks the method for offering food, one should present them according to this rite.
One should use red non-glutinous rice, roots and fruits, honey-water, honey, sugar, rice-flour cakes, and the like;
for those who hold the mantras of female deities and others, one should offer soup, cooked rice, bean stew, and so forth."
All sweet syrups, water, *praṇāmbhṛtaka*, *kaṃsa*, *patra-rasa*, and so forth, as well as various fruits—these foods should all be offered to the female deities (*strī-devatās*).
"One who seeks the supreme accomplishment and performs the ritual offerings of their own deity family should offer according to this method.

Regarding the various foods, roots, fruits, incenses, and so forth commonly discussed by the multitude—those that are abundant, highly esteemed, and possess exquisite flavors—one should seek such superior flavors for the sake of supreme accomplishment and present them as an offering."

As briefly explained above, the various methods for offering food each follow their respective families; the ritual procedures for the matters sought have all been set forth in summary. Should the flavors of food differ in other regions, one should observe their colors and tastes and offer them according to their kind.

"When about to present the food, first purify and smear the ground, sprinkle it everywhere with scented water, and thoroughly wash all the leaves. Then, spread upon them lotus leaves, *praseṇī* leaves, leaves from various milky trees, or new cotton cloth, and so forth; subsequently, serve the various delicacies using these leaves."
"For *śāntika*, one uses the leaves of aquatic plants, as well as the leaves of other extraordinary trees such as the plantain (*kadalī*);
for *pauṣṭika*, one uses the leaves of the *balādarka* tree, the *argha* tree, or whatever may be available at the time;
and for *abhicāruka*, one uses the leaves of female trees, namely:"
For instance, when the plantain first produces leaves, or with lotus leaves and leaves of the *kṣīravṛkṣa* tree;
furthermore, for the mantras of female ṛṣis, one uses *pātreya* leaves from a dried tree;
and for the terrestrial deities (*bhūcaradevatā*) and others, one uses grass.
One who seeks the superior, middling, or inferior dharmas must thoroughly understand and comprehend them.
First, smear and sprinkle the ground, then spread out various leaves; one should wash the hands, rinse the mouth, and swallow water, after which it is necessary to partake of the food.
First, serve the *śāṣṭika* rice;
next, serve fruits with round roots and long roots;
and next, serve various gruels.
Next, serve the soup and broth;
next, serve the milk and curd.
Serve these according to the original ritual procedure.
"If one constructs a maṇḍala or intends to accomplish various rites to attain the various states of realization, one should redouble the offerings of pure food, drink, flowers, fruits, and the like."
When first performing the recitation, one should offer whatever materials have been prepared and whatever flavors have been obtained, according to the specific ritual manual of that practice.
On the eighth, fourteenth, and fifteenth days of both the waxing and waning moon, as well as during solar and lunar eclipses or earthquakes, one should perform extensive offerings.
Furthermore, all items required for the homa fire ritual should first be prepared and placed before the presiding deity.
Whenever the practitioner wishes to eat, they should first set aside a portion of food and likewise place it before the Honored One.

If one intends to perform *homa* before eating, one should prepare the food in advance and set it out; having first arranged the offerings and prepared the meal, one should then commence the recitation. One must constantly offer flowers, medicinal herbs, and various foods, maintaining mindfulness without neglect or forgetfulness, always following the original ritual manual.
"If one recites at one time and makes offerings of various root fruits and food at one time;
or if one recites at two times and makes offerings at two times;
or if one recites at three times and makes offerings at three times—in accordance with the Dharma in this manner, one shall swiftly achieve accomplishment."

"If a practitioner of recitation fails to offer food and drink, thereby violating the rules of their own *kula*, that person will be beset by demonic obstacles, their body will lack vital luster, they will suffer from wind-disorders, dryness, hunger, and thirst, and will constantly harbor evil thoughts; they will be unable to achieve the mantras of their chosen deity (*iṣṭadevatā*), all because they fail to offer the fruit-offerings to the deity."
One should perform extensive offerings and present them to the principal deity and their retinue, following the previous instructions for the two months of the waxing and waning phases.
At the beginning of the recitation, on the aforementioned days, one should prepare *śāntika* food and discard it in the four directions at a distance from the place of recitation.

In this regard, it is not mentioned, or perhaps it is not applicable to this particular section; even if it were applicable, one should not seek higher accomplishment through inferior flavors, nor should one employ any types of prepared food that are foul-smelling or offensive.

One should constantly offer milk-rice; among the various classes [of mantras], those seeking the superior, middling, or inferior *śāntika* rites, as well as those who practice the general mantras of the devas, should perform worship in this manner.
If there is no food prepared according to the original injunctions, one should consecrate whatever has been obtained with the mantra of its respective family, reciting:
"This medicinal offering is fragrant and delicious, worthy of the Principal Deity; I now present it, praying that you will graciously accept it out of compassion."
The mantra for preparing food is:
"Aṭṭara aṭṭara sarvabhūtidhāra purati svāhā. This mantra is universally applicable to all three families.
"Recite the mantra after eating; offer the food while reciting the mantra you maintain.

Chapter Sixteen: Distinguishing the Attainments of Siddhi.
"I shall now further explain the attainments of siddhi for the three families."
To proceed through the air with sovereign mastery is the supreme accomplishment;
to conceal one's form and hide one's traces is the middling accomplishment;
[and to perform] various worldly affairs is the inferior accomplishment.
The three types of accomplishments are further distinguished according to the superior, middling, and inferior grades.

Regarding the supreme accomplishment methods of the three families: one attains the state of a vidyādhara who travels through the air, achieves the five supernormal powers (*pañcābhijñā*), and further accomplishes various other feats; or else, one attains the exhaustion of all outflows (*āsravakṣaya*);
or else, one attains the stage of a pratyekabuddha.
Some have realized the stages and grounds of a bodhisattva;
some understand all phenomena;
and some possess eloquence and extensive learning.
Some become vetālas; some become yakṣiṇīs;
or they obtain cintāmaṇis.
Alternatively, one may obtain inexhaustible treasures and possess such superior matters;
this is called the method of the "Superior-Superior" accomplishment (*uttarottara-siddhi*).
Within the three families (*trikula*), the treasury of accomplishment methods resides within the body, whereby one attains great power.
First, he overcame his former indolence to attain diligent vigor;
he entered the palace of the asuras to obtain the medicine of longevity;
and he became the celestial messenger Pāñcika.
Some are able to command spirits;
some are able to accomplish the attainment of the tree deity Śarabhaṇḍika;
and some achieve great learning, awakening to profound principles through what they have never heard before.
Or one may compound medicinal elixirs;

or, by merely applying [the medicine] to the feet and the crown of the head, one will travel great distances without fatigue. All such methods as described above are termed middling or superior accomplishments (*siddhi*).
"The methods for achieving lower success in the three families:
causing the multitude to behold one with joy, or subduing the masses;
or being able to punish evil persons, subdue hostile hosts, and accomplish other such inferior matters—these are called the methods for achieving lower-middle success."
"If one wishes to accomplish medicinal substances and the like, there are three types of accomplishment:
the appearance of flames is superior;
the appearance of smoke is middling."
Warmth is the lowest [level].
Furthermore, the mantras of the Noble Ones (ārya) constitute the supreme accomplishment;
those spoken by the devas constitute the middling accomplishment.
The mantras of the Worldly Deities (Laukika-devatā) constitute the lower accomplishment (*adhama-siddhi*).
Furthermore, the mantras of the Buddha Family (Buddha-kula) constitute the superior *siddhi*;
the mantras of the Lotus Family (Padma-kula) constitute the middling *siddhi*.
The mantras of the Vajra Family are for the lower siddhis.
If one desires to seek a lower accomplishment by means of a higher mantra, one will obtain the lower accomplishment;
or if one seeks a higher [accomplishment] by means of a lower mantra, one will obtain the higher accomplishment.
Alternatively, even if the upper and lower [mantras] are accomplished by means of the middle mantra, they likewise achieve accomplishment.
One should know that within a mantra these four virtues are complete, such that it can produce great fruits across all three divisions—superior, middling, and inferior—namely:
causing one to fulfill the stage of a Pratyekabuddha;
That is to say, bringing the ten stages of a bodhisattva to full completion and even attaining Buddhahood constitutes the great fruit and reward.
Furthermore, it constitutes great virtuous conduct; that is, being surrounded by a vast retinue of followers before and behind—one who fulfills such vows possesses great virtuous conduct.

Furthermore, one is able to abide long in various stations—namely, the station of a king, the station of a universal monarch (cakravartin), and the station of a long-lived immortal (ṛṣi)—and to fulfill such aspirations constitutes abiding for a long time.
The physical form and demeanor are vast and expansive, and its majestic radiance shines afar; it teaches the cultivation of the vast and expansive.
One who possesses these four virtues can achieve the superior grade even with a mantra of the inferior grade;
conversely, if these virtues are not present within a mantra of the superior grade, it functions as one of the inferior grade despite being of the superior grade.

"The mantras taught by the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas follow such a sequence; those spoken by many Buddhas and Bodhisattvas can accomplish even superior matters, despite belonging to an inferior grade."
"Among the mantras spoken by the Honored Ones and others, those that possess only a single purpose are as follows:
the śāntika rite, the pauṣṭika rite, and the ābhicāruka rite."
Although each possesses one of these factors, within them there are respectively superior, middling, and inferior grades; how could an inferior mantra possibly accomplish a superior task?
It is just as when exquisite lotus flowers emerge from blue mud—of this there is no doubt.
How could a mantra of superior-grade benevolence and compassion accomplish an inferior-grade accomplishment of wrath?
It is like white sandalwood, whose nature is cool; yet if it is struck by the wind and rubbed together, fire naturally arises—not without causes and conditions.
Although such variations do not follow a fixed sequence, all other *siddhis* remain subject to doubt.
"The *siddhi* of one's own body is the superior accomplishment;
the *siddhi* of medicinal herbs is the middling accomplishment."
The accomplishment (*siddhi*) of wealth and abundance is the inferior grade of attainment.

Furthermore, if a person has long practiced the recitation of an inferior mantra, even if they lack personal power, they may still seek it from the deity and achieve the superior grade through the deity's grace.

However, if one harbors doubt regarding a superior mantra, or if their recitation and offerings lack sincerity, then despite using a superior mantra, because of the lightness of their mind during recitation, it will result in an inferior accomplishment.

Therefore, know that the practice of recitation depends entirely upon the mind. For instance, among the various devas there are those who are poor, and within the ranks of the pretas there are those who are wealthy and powerful; since this is known to be so for them, it is likewise for mantras. Every single mantra possesses the three levels of *siddhi*—namely, superior, middling, and inferior—and by reciting with a sincere heart, one shall attain *siddhi*.

Chapter Seventeen: The Chapter on Invocation *Susiddhikara Sūtra*, Chapter Seventeen: The Chapter on Invocation "Furthermore, if one wishes to enter the chamber of the tutelary deity (*iṣṭadevatā*), one should first gaze upon the countenance of the Honored One and join the ten fingers and toes, slightly bowing the head. Next, one should place pure water in a vessel according to the specific rite being performed, set out the primary offering flowers, and further provide scented ointment. Following the original ritual manual, one should perform the *argha* (water-offering) and burn incense to fumigate it; one should recite the mantra seven times over the *argha*. Then, having performed the invocation, one should make offerings according to the ritual law."
“The vessel for the *argha* offering should be made of gold;
or else of copper;
or it may be fashioned from stone.”
Some were made of earth or wood;
some were fashioned from shells;
others were made of bamboo.
Alternatively, one may use lotus leaves to fashion vessels,
or leaves from milk-producing trees.
Regarding the *argha* vessels and other implements mentioned above, one must understand the proper sequence when employing them.
"If for *śāntika* one should use a white vessel;
for *pauṣṭika*, a yellow vessel;
and for *abhicāruka*, a black vessel."
To accomplish the superior, middling, and inferior *siddhis*, one should employ them according to what was previously explained.
For performing *śāntika* rites, place a small amount of barley in the *argha* vessel;
for *pauṣṭika* rites, one should include sesame seeds.
For ābhicāruka rites, one should use *sūma*;
furthermore, for śāntika rites, place milk;
for pauṣṭika rites, place curd.
For an *abhicāruka* rite, one should place cow’s urine or one's own blood;

for rites that are universally applicable, one should use rice blossoms, unguents, flowers, sesame seeds, and rings of *kuśa* grass. One should use a vessel of refined copper to hold the *arghya* offering; if such a vessel is unavailable, whatever is at hand may be used for universal purposes.
"At the time of invocation, one should employ the mantra of the Vidyārāja of the relevant family and the mudrā.

If the specific ritual manual contains a previously taught invocation mantra, that should be used and no other; first invoke the honored deity of the family, and next invoke the consort of the Vidyārāja; this should be done in the same manner for all three families.
If the ritual manual lacks an invocation mantra, one should use the mantras of the Vidyārājas and others to perform the invocation."
Although the *mūlakalpa* states that the mantras for invocation are of inferior rank, how could it be appropriate to invoke the Lord of the Family [with them]?
If one invokes using the mantras of the *mūlakalpa*, success will be swiftly attained; one should not raise objections.
If the *mūlakalpa* contains mantras for invocation and dismissal, at the time of invocation, this mantra-lord shall go to the presence of the Lord of the Family and request as follows:
"Now, so-and-so requests you for such-and-such a matter... When dispatching them, it is likewise:
"The task having been completed, may the Venerable One bear witness and depart as you please."

"The mantra of the Queen of the Vidyārāja is used to invite the female seers (ṛṣikā) and others; the mantra of the Vidyārāja is used to invite the lords of mantras (vidyārājādhipati). If there are lords of mantras who do not accept the invitation of the Vidyārāja’s mantra, one must use the mantra of the Queen of the Vidyārāja to invite them."

"As stated in other sections, when offering *argha* water, one should recite the mantra: once for a superior [offering], three times for a middling one, seven times for an inferior one, and twenty-one times for the smallest."

Regarding the *argha* ritual rules explained above: first, with both knees touching the ground, one must place the hands upon a ring of pure *kuśa* grass, hold up the *argha*, and while incense is being burned, make this request:

"I humbly entreat you, Venerable One, to descend to this site of practice by virtue of your original vow; I pray that you will look upon me with compassion and accept this *argha* and these humble offerings."
“There is a Lord of Mantras named Vikiraṇa-krodha, who does not accept the invocations of other mantras; one must use the mantra he himself taught to bring about the descent of the invoked deity.

His retinue likewise does not accept the invitations of other mantras; one should not use the mantras of his retinue to summon them, but rather employ the *cittamantra*, or the *mūlamantra*, or the mantra spoken by the Vidyārājñī to perform the invocation.”

The Family Heart Mantra is universally applicable to all three families; when performing the invocation, one should cause [the deity] to descend by adding the syllable "ĪḤI," which is even more secret and swiftly fulfills one's wishes.
When making the invitation, one should prostrate with a sincere heart and address them three times:
"O Great Compassionate One!
We pray that you will descend to this ritual site in accordance with your original vow."
"If one lacks a sincere heart and merely recites many times—

even if the mantras themselves are performed with earnest diligence— it is considered the highest *siddhi* to offer the *argha* vessel by holding it with both hands and placing it upon the crown of the head;
to place it at the center of the heart is the middling *siddhi*."
Placing it at the navel constitutes the lower siddhi.
First, one should visualize the painted image of the deity: if the image is standing, the mantra-reciter should also stand when making the request;
if the image is seated, one should also sit when making the request.
Furthermore, one should observe the posture of that image—whether it be bent or standing—and likewise adopt such a stance while making the invitation.

At the time of the invitation, first observe the direction in which the Honored One resides and face that direction to invite them; then, turn your body and place the *argha* offering before the honored image.

Furthermore, there are secret visualizations for summoning [deities] at various locations such as those for *śāntika* (pacifying) rites; or, at other times, when one obtains flowers or fruits that accord with the intent of the *iṣṭadevatā*, one should first perform an invitation and then offer them.

When making the invitation, join the fingers and palms of the hands according to their respective directions and invoke with a heart of utmost sincerity; alternatively, invite them by holding up an *argha* vessel with both hands, and thereafter arrange and present whatever offerings have been obtained.
"If one wishes to accomplish superior, middling, or inferior matters, as well as the *śāntika* rite, one must in all cases employ mantras and *mudrās* to perform the invocation."
If obstacles arise during the performance of various rites;
or if Māras cause disturbances;

or if the patient’s condition worsens—at such times, because the circumstances are urgent and one cannot wait to prepare the *argha* vessel, one should immediately apply the mind to invoke the *iṣṭadevatā* and perform the rite of expulsion (*vidhūnana*).

As previously explained, one should offer argha water according to the scale of the rite, whether for the purpose of accomplishment or for urgent matters such as emergencies, invoking [the deity] with a sincere heart.

Furthermore, if anyone wishes to take refuge in and rely upon the venerable ones of the various families (kula), they should constantly perform the ritual rules for invocation; by doing so, the practitioner will swiftly attain accomplishment.

Chapter 18: The Chapter on Offerings (*Pūjā*) from the Susiddhikara Sūtra. "Furthermore, having performed the invitation (*āvāhana*), one should, according to the specific family (*kula*) or the various rites (*karma*), observe their magnitude and perform the offerings in accordance with the ritual rules."
Having thus invited him, they spoke these words:
"Welcome, Venerable One!
Out of compassion for us, you have descended to this site of practice; we pray that you will further show us mercy by taking this seat and accepting our humble offerings."
Again, arising with a sincere heart and repeatedly prostrating, he addressed the Honored One, saying:
"The Great Compassionate One has condescended to appear out of pity and to fulfill my original vow; it was not within my power to petition the Honored One myself!"
"In this manner, one should rely on this during all three periods.
As previously stated, one must prepare the offerings;
first, present the scented ointment."
Next, offer flowers and so forth;
then present incense for burning;
next, present food and drink.
Next, light the lamps.

Following the proper sequence, employ the mantras of the Wrathful Kings (krodharāja) so that these offering substances are all rendered pure and pleasing to the mind. Recite the specific mantra for each color and present the fragrant unguents (gandha), then list their names individually. As previously explained, offer the arghya water; likewise, the flowers, incense, food, and drink should all be treated in accordance with this.
If one has no unguents, incense, flowers, or food and drink to offer, one should simply recite the original mantra of the deity and perform this mudrā to present the offering.
The petition stated:
"Offerings cannot be obtained; I offer only my sincere heart.
Later, when he performed the *argha* offering, because of his sincere heart, his wishes were swiftly fulfilled.
"Beyond these, there are four types of offerings that are universally applicable across all sections and in all contexts.
First is the joining of palms;
second is the offering of argha water."
Third, employing mantras and mudrās;
fourth, merely directing the mind.
Among these virtuous practices, one should act according to one's capacity; alternatively, within long-term offerings, there is no fault in simply directing the mind.
As the World-Honored One has taught, among all dharmas and practices, the mind is the foremost; if one can focus the mind and offer worship, all aspirations will be fulfilled.

"If one wishes to accomplish other matters, one should dispatch those who create obstacles; for if they are not removed, there is fear that harm may later ensue. Therefore, one must first perform the rite of dispatching [obstacles], reciting the wrathful mantra or the mantra for accomplishing all matters belonging to the relevant family."

Having dispelled the obstacles, one should next recite the mantra of the honored deity of the respective family (*kula*). Then, with the *homa* and wheel hand-mudrās, universally invoke the deity into the water.
The mantra for invoking the Fire God (*Agni*) of the Buddha Family is:
*Vyaśva vyaśva bhoḥ naya svāhā.* Recite this mantra three times to summon the Fire God.
The *homa* mantra for offering burnt food is:
"Oṃ anaye ṣvāhā vahanāya jñapaya jñapi nibodhaya svāhā. Next, holding cow’s ghee, burn it with this mantra one recitation at a time, performing the offering to the Fire God three times.
The Vajra-family Wrathful Vajra Mantra:
“Oṃ kili kili vajra-krodha hūṃ phaṭ. Recite this mantra once for each morsel of food and offer it into the fire; by performing this rite, one dispels all obstructors dwelling within the earth.
Furthermore, one should sprinkle flowers and other offerings with this mantra, or with the mantra of the specific deity of that family;

then, using the Kilikīla-krūra-vidyā-mantra along with its mudrā, one should recite the mantra while forming the mudrā with the left hand to seal and purify the unguents, incense, food, flowers, and so forth, thereby removing all impurities.

For the sake of purifying oneself, one should cup fragrant water in the right hand, gaze at the water while reciting the heart-mantra, and pour it over the crown of one’s head to purify and remove all defilements.

Furthermore, using the Sarvakarmasiddhi-mantra along with the Krodha-mantra, one should sprinkle scented water upon the seat with the mantra for the purpose of purifying it; moreover, by reciting it seven times and sprinkling it over the site and its boundaries, all impurities are removed and it becomes pure.
The Kīlikīla Mantra:

“Oṃ kili kili vajra vajri budhanta bandha huṃ phaṭ. Having protected the site with this aforementioned mantra, one should bind the realm of space (*ākāśadhātu*). One should then hold incense while reciting the Susiddhi mantra that follows; by fumigating the air with its fragrance, all impurities and evils are removed, and it becomes pure.
The Susiddhi Mantra:

"Oṃ susiddhikari jvali-dāna mumoradaye jvala jvala bandha hana hana huṃ phaṭ. This Susiddhi mantra of the Vajra Family is universally applicable for all rites and for the purpose of binding the boundary of space (khecarī).
The mantra for binding the spatial boundary of the Buddha Family is:
"Oṃ jambhala huṃ hūṃ. This mantra for binding the spatial boundary of the Buddha Family applies exclusively to its own family.
The mantra for binding the space-element (ākāśadhātu) of the Lotus Family is:
“Oṃ padmini bhagavati mohaya mohaya jñāna-mohana svāhā. This mantra for binding the space-element of the Lotus Family belongs exclusively to this family.
"Next, one should sprinkle the various directions with perfumed water using the Family Heart Mantra (kulahṛdaya-mantra).

Then, using either the Root Mantra or the Heart Mantra of the Vidyārāja, or the Heart Mantra of a messenger of the Mantrarāja—taking whichever is appropriate—one should bind the boundaries of the directions (digbandha).

Alternatively, one may perform the boundary-binding (sīmābandha) using these various Heart Mantras; the place thus bound will be like a wall erected, and the sages and devas of that particular Family will constantly provide protection, such that no one can create obstacles."
If there are various ritual matters involving conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛtadharma*), they should be dispelled by relying on the method of Amṛtakuṇḍalin.
Furthermore, there are five kinds of protective rites that should always be performed within the chamber of the maṇḍala; namely:
the Vajra Wall, the Vajra City, the Vajra Stake, the Wrathful Kīlikīla, and the Wrathful Amṛtakuṇḍalin.
The mantra of the Vajraprākāra (Vajra-Wall) of the Family Mother: “Oṃ sara sara vajravara-kāla hūṃ phaṭ.
The mantra of the Vajrapura (Vajra-City): “Oṃ miṣe pramardana kṣa vajrapañjara hūṃ phaṭ. The mantra of the Vajrakīla (Vajra-Stake):
“Oṃ vīra-kīla hūṃ phaṭ. The mantra of the wrathful Kīlikīla: “Oṃ kili kili vajra hūṃ phaṭ. The mantra of the wrathful Amṛtakuṇḍalī:

“Tāranāya | namo vajra-krodhāya mahā-bala-parākramāya | buddha-mitrāṇa-vināśanāya | oṃ hulu hulu tiṣṭha tiṣṭha bandha bandha hana hana amṛte hūṃ phaṭ. If there are such mantras for the vajra wall within the primary ritual (*mūla-vidhi*), they should be bound repeatedly.
When all matters have been concluded, one should next perform the recitation (*japa*). At the time of recitation, one should first recite the Mother-mantra (*mātṛ-mantra*) of the respective family.
The Mother-mantra of the Buddha Family (*buddhakula*):
*Jvala tiṣṭha siddhalocane sarvārtha-sādhani svāhā.* The Mother-mantra of the Lotus Family (*padmakula*):
"Oṃ kaje mike kaje kaṅka je kaṣṭa mike kaṣṭakaṅka kaje bhagavati mārīye svāhā. The Vidyā of the Mother of the Vajra Family:

"Namo lokeśvarāya śrīye | Namaḥ saṃkara-santika-raṣṭa-raṣṭa-raṣṭa-nigata-ya raṣṭi-kuje svāhā. If one first recites this Vidyā of the Mother, it can protect the principal deity (iṣṭadevatā), eliminate all sins, remove all calamities and obstacles, and bring about correspondence with the gateway of siddhi.
However, reciting the Maṃjuśrī mantra of the Buddha Family is also effective for both families; at the beginning and end of the recitation, the various devas will provide increased protection.
If the mantra has already been explained within its own specific ritual (vidhi), one should recite it while first recollecting this [Maṃjuśrī mantra];
or, if there is a particularly superior mantra unique to that specific ritual, one should likewise recite that first without complication.

Regarding the sequence of offerings described above, including all matters such as the removal of impurities, the protection and purification of the site, and the binding of the boundary, these should all be performed at the time of first undertaking the recitation, during the performance of ritual acts, and whenever performing rites such as the *śāntika* (pacifying) and others.
"Whether by means of the mantra of the Lord of the Family,
or the heart-mantra (hṛdaya) of the Family,
or the mantra of the King of All Mantras;
One may use either the King of Mantras of Susiddhi or the Mantra of All Affairs.
These five types of mantras are present throughout the three families; for whatever task one performs, one should select one from the appropriate family and employ it accordingly.

Regarding what is called protecting oneself and protecting one's companions: through the ritual procedures of invitation, sprinkling water, purification, and boundary-binding (*sīmābandha*), one sustains oneself according to the Dharma. If these words are incomplete, they are for the purpose of increasing power;
for the purpose of subduing mantras;

for the purpose of awakening; and for other matters not explicitly described, one should likewise select any one from among the five *mātṛ* mantras of the relevant family and employ it, whereby one shall attain *siddhi*.

"The Family Heart Mantra can protect both the deity and one's own body. When protecting the body, one should recite it three or seven times, binding the hair on the crown of the head into a single topknot."
If one is a renunciant, one may tie the corners of the *kāṣāya*;
or tie a cord and fasten it to protect the body;
or, by reciting mantras while touching the five places with the index finger, one also accomplishes protection of the body, namely:
On the crown of the head, the forehead, both shoulders, below the throat, and over the heart.
One may use either ox-gallstone or white mustard seeds.
Alternatively, one may take any one of the *arghya* waters and use it to protect the body.
If performing an *ābhicāruka* rite, one should protect oneself by reciting the mantra of the Lord of the Family;
if performing a *śāntika* rite, one should protect oneself by reciting the mantra of Krodhavajra.
If one performs the pauṣṭika rite, one should protect it by employing both the mantra of the Family Lord (kuleśvara) and the mantra of the Wrathful Vajra.
If the practitioner becomes afraid when the Mantra Lord appears, they should use the mantra of the Family Lord to protect themselves;
however, whenever performing any ritual activity, one should always use these two mantras—the mantra of the Family Lord and the wrathful mantra—to protect oneself.

"When the recitation is completed, one should perform the dismissal (*visarjana*). At the time of dismissal, one should protect the Lord of Mantras or the Lord of the Family (*kula-nātha*), using either the mantra, the Family Mother (*kula-mātṛ*), or the Family Heart (*kula-hṛdaya*);
furthermore, one should protect oneself and then act as one pleases."

"If one must go to a defiled place, such as an impure location, for some necessary business, one should first recite the Ukkośama mantra and form the mudrā to seal the five places [of the body] before proceeding as one pleases; furthermore, one must constantly recite the mantra without neglecting it."
Prior to bathing, one should recite the mantra of the Vajra Family to protect oneself; this should not be neglected until the bath is completed.
The mantra of the Vajra Family is that of the wrathful deity Amṛtakuṇḍalī.
When eating, one should protect the body by reciting the mantra of the Lord of the Family;
when about to lie down, one should protect the body by reciting the mantra of the Mother of the Family.

"If, while performing various rites, one forgets to perform these methods of protection, it will cause demons to arise. To eliminate these demons, one should quickly recite the mantra of the Vidyārāja of the relevant Family to guard oneself; thus, no demonic faction shall find an opportunity."
Having fully performed the aforementioned methods for protecting the body, binding the boundaries, and other rites, one should thereafter collect the mind and recite with composure.

As for the seat upon which the practitioner sits while reciting, it should be made of blue *kuśa* grass; the seat should be four finger-widths high, two spans wide, and sixteen finger-widths long. Such a seat should be used both at the time of the initial recitation and during the entire course of the mantra-holding practice.
Alternatively, one may use *kāśa* grass, or other green grasses and the like;

or, according to the ritual of the specific family (*kula*), it is most essential to take a milky tree for this purpose. One should fashion a seat from it, with dimensions as described above, and carefully trim and prepare it.
Alternatively, one may use various leaves;
or, as described above, fashion them from branches and stems according to the ritual procedures for attending upon [the deity], taking branches and leaves to serve as a seat.
Upon this seat, sit in the full lotus posture (*paryaṅka*) and perform the *śāntika* (pacifying) supreme accomplishment rite.
Sitting cross-legged in the *paryaṅka* posture, one performs the *sādhana* of the middle accomplishment (*puṣṭika*);
sitting with both feet hanging down, one performs the lower accomplishment (*abhicāruka*).

Once the offerings are completed, one should arouse a sincere mind to praise the Buddha, then the Dharma, then the Saṃgha; next, praise Avalokiteśvara, and finally praise the Great Powerful Vajra of the Vidyārāja.
The verse says:
"O World-Honored One of Great Compassion!
You skillfully guide all beings;
I now prostrate in homage to the ocean of merit and virtue that upholds blessings;
I now prostrate in homage to the Dharma of True Suchness and Śamatha, Which can purify the poisons of greed and hatred, And skillfully eliminate all evil destinies.
To the Saṅgha who has attained liberation through the Dharma,
who dwells well in the stages of training,
and who is the cause of supreme merit— I now prostrate in homage.
O Greatly Compassionate Avalokiteśvara!
Praised by all Buddhas, you are able to generate manifold merits; to you I now pay homage with my head bowed low.
O Great Powerful Wrathful Body!
Excellent King of Vidyādharas;
you who subdue those difficult to subdue—I now prostrate and pay homage to you.

"Having thus offered sincere praise to the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas, one should again join the palms and, with a heart of profound reverence, praise the marks and excellences (*lakṣaṇa-vyañjana*) and meritorious virtues of other Buddhas and Bodhisattvas; the verses for this praise should employ those spoken by the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas themselves, rather than composing them oneself."
Having finished the praise, one should arouse a heart of utmost sincerity and repent for all transgressions, saying:
"I take refuge in the Buddhas, World-Honored Ones, Arhats, Noble Sangha, and all Bodhisattvas throughout the worlds of the ten directions!"

We testify that from the past until our present lives, our minds have been shrouded by afflictions as we have long wandered through birth and death; covered by greed, hatred, and delusion, we have committed various evil karmas—whether toward the Buddha, the Dharma, Bodhisattvas, the noble Sangha, our parents and elders, all sentient beings, or those with virtue and those without—regardless of the circumstances in which these were done. All such sinful karma, whether committed by ourselves, incited in others, or witnessed with rejoicing, and all the various transgressions accumulated extensively through the actions of body, speech, and mind, we now repent with a sincere heart before all the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas.

I repent of all the various sins I have committed, as known by all the Buddhas, and with a heart of sincere resolve, I take refuge for the rest of my life in the Triple Gem of the Buddha, Dharma, and Sangha—the true path to Nirvana—and I take refuge in the Three Jewels in order to eliminate all suffering of sentient beings.

Having thus taken refuge and prostrated with the crown of one’s head, one rejoices and leaps for joy, generating the bodhicitta and seeking the supreme siddhi of the nectar of liberation—the fruit of Buddhahood.
I shall rescue and deliver the immeasurable suffering of sentient beings in the world, causing them to leave the evil realms behind and eliminate all afflictions;
I shall cause them to attain liberation from all forms of suffering and manifold torments.
Now, having given rise to great compassion and resolved upon bodhicitta, you take refuge for the sake of sentient beings;
you act as a protector for those who have no protector,
and as a guide for those who have lost their way.
I shall grant fearlessness to sentient beings who are terrified;
for the sake of bringing peace and happiness to those afflicted by suffering, I shall eliminate the afflictions of all sentient beings.

With a mind that aspires toward supreme deeds throughout the past, present, and future, I shall cultivate all wholesome karmas and the six *pāramitās*, dedicating all such merit entirely to bestowing it upon all sentient beings so that they may enter the right path, ascend together to the wondrous fruit, and swiftly attain the Buddha-way. Until reaching Bodhi, I shall never give rise to indolence; I shall resolve upon the Bodhicitta, compassionately mindful of sentient beings, and give rise to a heart of great loving-kindness (*maitrī*).
When will their manifold sufferings be extinguished?

For the sake of purifying the mind, they should constantly maintain the six recollections (*ṣaḍ-anusmṛti*), focusing the mind on a single object without distraction, and remaining free from self-clinging (*ātmagrāha*).
Furthermore, as the Buddhas of the past and present have made their vows, one should likewise make vows to generate all pure karma and vow that sentient beings may achieve all virtues.

Moreover, one should vow that the merits produced in the past and present may cause all sentient beings to obtain inexhaustible wealth and be able to practice generosity, increase wisdom, and achieve great patience; that they may constantly cultivate wholesome qualities, possess the knowledge of recollecting past lives, and harbor great compassion in their hearts.
"May all classes of living beings, in whatever place they are born, be endowed with the matters mentioned above.
Next, one should join the palms and prostrate to the Honored Lord of the Family, recollecting the Vidyārāja, and then perform all ritual activities according to the prescribed rules.
First, take the rosary with the right hand, place it in the left hand, join the palms to support it, and while contemplating the Vidyārāja, count the beads and recite the mantra.
The Mantra for Purifying the Rosary of the Buddha Family:
*Oṃ abja-miñje siddhisiddhāya svāhā.* The Mantra for Purifying the Rosary of the Lotus Family:
"Oṃ amṛtatejāye śrīye śrīmālini svāhā. The mantra for purifying the rosary of the Vajra Family: "Oṃ kili kili glūri svāhā.

With the right hand, press the tip of the ring finger with the thumb, extend the middle and little fingers straight, and slightly bend them; place the index finger upon the side of the upper joint of the middle finger. The left hand is likewise positioned. Holding the rosary with the right hand is used for all purposes.
"If it is an ābhicāruka [rite], one should hold up the thumb and form the mudrā of counting the rosary beads.
Bodhi seeds are used for the Buddha family;
lotus seeds are used for the Avalokiteśvara family."
The *ruṇāla* seed-beads are for use with the Vajra [family];
these types of rosaries are the most excellent for each of the three families, and one should hold them during all recitations.
Alternatively, one may use wood from the khadira tree;
or seeds of the tāla tree;
or use earth beads.
Or using conch beads;
or using crystal; or using pearls;
Or using ivory beads;
or using red pearls;
or various maṇi jewels;

Alternatively, one may use a *ghuṇṭhikā* (neck-bead) or other seeds from grasses, each according to its respective family (*kula*), selecting them based on their color and type for recitation and retention.
"If performing an *abhicāra* rite, one should use heads as rosary beads, because they bring swift accomplishment and serve to provide protection and increase efficacy."
The *dhāraṇī* for holding the rosary of the Buddha Family:
"Oṃ namo bhagavatyai siddhe siddhe sādhye siddhalatve svāhā. The *dhāraṇī* for holding the rosary of the Lotus Family:
"Oṃ sumatiśrīye padmaratne svāhā. The *dhāraṇī* for holding the rosary of the Vajra Family:
"Oṃ vajra-īdan-jaye svāhā. Recite this using the aforementioned bead and mudrā, each according to its respective family (kula).
When reciting, place the rosary at your heart, neither too high nor too low. When holding the rosary, slightly lower your head and, with a sincere mind, prostrate to the Triple Gem;
next, to the Eight Great Bodhisattvas;
and next, to the retinue of the Vidyārāja.

Next, one should maintain the recitation of the mantra while visualizing it as if it were right before one’s eyes; thus, with sincere devotion, one must not allow the mind to wander toward other objects.

Regarding mantras that begin with the syllable *oṃ* and the word *nāmasakalāya*, one should perform *śāntika* (pacifying) and *pauṣṭika* (prosperity) recitations with a tranquil mind, reciting them slowly or mentally.

As for those mantras that end with the syllables *hūṃ phaṭ*, one should know that these all require a sharp, urgent sound for the performance of *abhicāruka* (subjugating/destroying) and other wrathful recitations.
"One should examine the number of syllables in the mantras of the three families.
If there are fifteen syllables, one should recite fifteen lakṣas;
if there are thirty-two syllables, one should recite three lakṣas; and for those exceeding this number, one should recite more than ten thousand times."
"When reciting for the first time, complete the aforementioned number of repetitions; then examine its categories as superior, middling, or inferior;
or its three types of matters;
or consider the explanations given by the Noble Ones."
It was spoken by the devas;
it was spoken by the devas who dwell upon the earth.
One should carefully examine its categories and recite and uphold it until accomplishment is attained.
If one does not first recite and maintain the full extent of the initial recitation, even the lower rites sought will not be accomplished, let alone the higher or middling *siddhi* attainments.
For this reason, one should generate a superior mind and first perform the recitation.

As previously explained regarding the initial recitation of any mantra, one should divide the total number of recitations into ten parts; once the recitation is complete, one should then pray to the Lord of Mantras for the causes and conditions of *siddhi*.
If at first there is no sign, one should again perform the second and third supplications from the beginning;
if a sign appears, one should then recite the mantra according to the ritual rules;
if no state of realization arises, one should abandon it and not recite.

The ritual for supplication is the same as the ritual for invocation. During the time of supplication, if one sees the Lord of Mantras turning his back and departing, or not speaking with one, in one's dream, one should begin the recitation anew; this should be done two or three times.
If, in the dream, one sees the Lord of Mantras speaking with one, it should be known that this person will achieve accomplishment before long.
If there is no such vision, one should not perform the recitation; if one were to force oneself to recite and maintain it, it may bring calamity upon others.

When first beginning the recitation, start in a clean and secluded place; from the first day of recitation until you are utterly exhausted, the number of repetitions must strictly follow the fixed requirement and must not be increased or decreased.
"Regarding the previously mentioned method of recitation during the three periods of the day:
one should perform the recitation during the first and last periods of the day; during the middle period, one should engage in bathing and the performance of various virtuous deeds.

Regarding the three periods of the night, it is the same as above; however, during the middle period, one should attend to matters of rest and recuperation, and perform the recitation during the final period of the night."
The *ābhicāruka* rite, the *āntardhāna* rite, and the *utthāpana* rite are said to be most excellent when performed during the night.
"If one performs recitation by day and homa by night;
or if one maintains recitation by night and performs homa by day, one should employ many medicinal substances."
If one performs *homa* before the recitation and again performs *homa* after the recitation is finished, this is the most excellent method.
As previously stated, one should perform *homa* with the ritual balls (*piṇḍa*) that have been prepared; whether before or after, one should always rely on this method for recitation and *homa*.

Alternatively, if within a particular rite success is attained by performing *homa* alone, one should know that it is nonetheless necessary to recite the mantra. If one acts in this manner, the vidyās will be delighted and the signs of the rite’s efficacy will be easily accomplished.
"The practitioner of recitation should not give rise to anger;
should not seek sensual pleasures;
and should not disparage themselves."
One does not give rise to resentment through lack of diligent effort;
one does not fail to seek with excessive diligence;
and one does not give rise to contempt.

"When reciting, do not speak of other matters; though the body may become utterly exhausted, do not let it slacken. Restrain all evil impulses and do not think of worldly talk. Do not abandon the *iṣṭadevatā*, and even if you see extraordinary signs, do not be startled by them;
while reciting, do not discriminate among various appearances."
"When the recitation is completed, one should recite the mantra of the Lord of the Family, or the mantra of the Mother of the Family;
by reciting these mantras, one shall obtain protection and ensure that the rites of the Family are not transgressed."

Having completed the recitation according to this primary rite, or even if one has exceeded the prescribed number, one should have no fear; rather, with a sincere heart, one should offer this supplication:
"I have fulfilled the number of recitations according to this primary rite; I pray that you, O Venerable One, will accept this as my witness and grant me instructions within my dreams."

"When reciting with right mindfulness, if one coughs, becomes drowsy, yawns, or omits a syllable of the mantra, one should immediately rise, go to water, and perform the ritual of sprinkling for purification (*prokṣaṇa*). Even if one has counted the beads and is short by only one round, upon encountering such an impediment, once the purification is complete, one must begin again from the very beginning; because the recitation has been interrupted, each instance requires starting anew from the start."
When you have nearly finished counting the beads while reciting the mantra, perform one prostration; when you have completed the cycle and begun again,
perform another prostration before the painted image or before the stūpa.
Alternatively, at the place of sitting or wherever one recites, for every single circuit of the rosary, gaze upon the countenance of the Honored One and perform a single prostration.
Once the recitation is finished, settle the mind in pure contemplation, either visualizing the mantra or its presiding deity.

During the three periods of recitation—namely, the first, middle, and last watches of the night—one should apply the mind with sincerity; the number of recitations should remain uniform across all sessions, neither increasing nor decreasing.
One should bathe at the three periods, smear the ground [with fragrant paste], offer flowers, scented water, and various other offerings, and remove withered flowers.
"One should possess the three robes.
Furthermore, one's inner robe should be washed three times a day; once it is dry, scented, and purified by sprinkling, one may perform each of these acts as permitted during each respective period."

One should set aside separate garments for sleeping and bathing, changing these undergarments at these two times; one should wash such clothing once daily, and when dry, it is permitted to fumigate or sprinkle it with perfumes.
"Offer the water vessel and bowl, washing and cleaning them at the three times of day; once withered flowers have been removed, replace them with fresh ones;
and at the three times, constantly recite Mahāyāna sūtras such as the *Prajñāpāramitā* and perform the consecration of caityas and the painting of maṇḍalas."

First, recite the mantra of service; once this is completed, if you have not yet obtained the requested boon, you must not neglect it for even one session or two sessions, nor even for a single morning. You should continue the recitation without interruption.
