Furthermore, recite the Vajra-Railing mantra one hundred times over iron filings and likewise fashion three-pronged vajras; place these horizontally upon the upright vajras, encircling the maṇḍala, to serve as the vajra railing.
"The gate of the outer maṇḍala is protected by the mantra of Kuntali and the vajra-mudrā;
the second enclosure gate is protected by Hārītī;
and the gate of the central courtyard is protected by Aparājita."
These gate-protectors are common to all three families, or alternatively, one may protect all three gates with a single one.
These three holy beings all crush all that is heterodox and cannot be destroyed; this is the secret protection for accomplishing the ritual objects.
"In the center of that platform, five precious objects are to be buried.

However, when constructing a maṇḍala at a place where people have gathered, those five precious objects should not be buried; rather, they should simply be placed beneath the object being constructed. The same applies when constructing a maṇḍala in a courtyard, inside a room, or within a Buddha hall."
"In these five locations, it is sufficient merely to recite [the mantra] and sprinkle scented water; purification is thereby accomplished without the need for digging the ground.
If one performs this rite within one's own regular recitation chamber, accomplishment will be swiftly attained."
One should not perform the rites for accomplishment within caves, nor should one do so in dilapidated dwellings.

When wishing to construct a maṇḍala, during the evening seven days prior, with a heart of profound reverence, one should visualize all the honored deities as if they were standing before one’s eyes and address this invitation:

"O all honored deities within the three families, and all the deities and their retinues within this treasury, I have long practiced recitation, performed homa, and maintained my observance of the precepts. By means of these mantras, I offer worship to you all; I pray that on the seventh day hence you will descend to this ritual site. Out of compassion for me, accept this humble offering, and through your great loving-kindness and compassion, grant me success."

In this manner, continuing until the seventh day has passed, one should perform the ritual after making offerings and petitions. Furthermore, with *argha* water, flowers, incense, food and drink, and hymns of praise, one should offer special worship to a guardian deity (*lokapāla*) of one direction every evening; this should be done likewise for all three directions.
Furthermore, one should apply incense to the hands and recite the mantra while pressing the object with those hands to perform the invocation;
again, one may invoke by fumigating the object with burning incense;
and yet again, one may observe a fast, select an auspicious day, briefly construct a maṇḍala, and use articles for the invocation.

"Alternatively, one may construct a circular maṇḍala using only a single color; it should have only one gate, with an eight-petaled lotus flower placed in its center measuring two cubits in size, while the remaining outer precincts are made according to one's preference for their dimensions."
"First, place the lords of the three families within the inner courtyard.
To the north of the western gate, place Maheśvara and his consort.
To the right of the Buddha, place Mātṛceta; to his left, place Buddhalocanā."
Next, place Maṃśrī to the right of Avalokiteśvara and the Six-Armed One to his left;
next, place Maṅgala to the right of Vajra and the Heart of the Vidyārāja to his left;
and to the south of the western gate, place the wrathful Kṛtānta and the Vajrāṅkuśa. All those mentioned above are to be installed within the inner court.
"Next, in the outer enclosure, one should place the deities of the eight directions and the lords of mantras who are capable of accomplishing all tasks.
Furthermore, the lords of mantras whom one’s heart reveres, from both the inner and outer enclosures, should all be joyfully installed."
Place the Tāriṇī at the northern side of the outer gate and the Aparājita at the southern side of the gate; invite and make offerings to each with their respective heart-mantras.
Place the articles for accomplishment upon lotuses and offer them as worship.
Alternatively, one may place a full *karṣa* jar upon a lotus flower and set the article for accomplishment upon it;
or one may place a casket upon a lotus flower with the object contained within;
or one may place an earthenware vessel upon a lotus flower with the object contained within.
If one places the object upon a lotus flower within a floral womb, presses it with the hand, and recites the mantra over it one thousand or one hundred times;
thereafter, reciting the mantra, one hurls the flower onto the object;
and finally, one fumigates it by burning incense of *guggulu* mixed with clarified butter (*sarpis*).
Next, one should again lightly sprinkle scented water upon the objects;

next, one should recite the vidyā-mantra of the Mother Vidyārājñī over those objects, and for each of the deities present in the maṇḍala, one should recite their respective mantras over those objects.
"Next, perform the homa with cow ghee;
or use cow's milk, or a mixture of ghee, honey, and sesame seeds for the homa, followed by the homa of *kaṭhinī*."

All items mentioned in this primary ritual should be subjected to homa; for each, one should perform homa extensively with all the mantras contained within the maṇḍala, and for each, one should consecrate the items by sprinkling them with perfumed water while reciting the respective mantra.
"Just as the methods for illuminating objects were previously explained, one should likewise perform the recitation here.

Looking at the object with one's own eyes while mentally reciting the mantra, by performing this rite, the ritual object becomes successfully invoked; indeed, by applying this method of invocation to any object whatsoever, one will swiftly attain accomplishment."
"Furthermore, one should perform every single offering and sacrificial rite belonging to this primary method in its entirety.
This ritual of invitation within the maṇḍala also applies to the upholding of substances and the illumination of substances;
if one performs the accomplishment (*sādhana*) therein, those who create obstacles shall find no opportunity, and it also applies to the purification of substances."
According to the method of empowerment, it also extends to the empowerment itself; its substance likewise extends to the empowerment of one's own person.
This is the secret, supreme maṇḍala capable of accomplishing all matters; if this rite is performed, there is nothing that cannot be achieved.
Chapter Thirty-Six: The Ritual for Amending Deficiencies in the Susiddhikara Sūtra. "I shall now explain the ritual for amending deficiencies."
Having taken up the object of practice, one should bathe three times daily;
perform offerings and homa three times a day while pressing the object with the hand;
change clothes three times a day; abstain from food on festival days; and all methods such as making offerings must be increased accordingly.
Perform prostrations, repentance, sympathetic joy, entreaty, and the making of vows during the three periods of the day;
recite scriptures and construct maṇḍalas during the three periods;
and take refuge and receive the precepts during the three periods.
By protecting oneself during the three periods [of the day], one will certainly achieve accomplishment through performing the rite in this manner.

"Alternatively, if a deficiency occurs due to negligence, one should immediately recite the Mother of the Family mantra twenty-one times to fulfill the requirement; if this rite is omitted, accomplishment will likewise be deficient.

Or, if there is a deficiency, one must further recite it one hundred thousand times and again construct this maṇḍala to compensate for the prior omission, only after which may one proceed to achieve accomplishment."
"As for the square of that maṇḍala, place four gates at the four corners and distribute the boundary lines as previously described.
Place the Buddha in the east;
on the right side place the Buddha’s ūrṇā-kośa (hair-treasure), on the left side place the Buddha’s śakti (lance/spear), and on the right side place the Buddha’s maitrī (loving-kindness)."
On the left place Buddhalocanā; on the right place Buddhakṣetrarāja-uṣṇīṣa.
On the left place Sitātapatrā-uṣṇīṣa; on the right place Tejorāśi.
On the left place Vijayā-uṣṇīṣa; on the right place Abhyudgata-uṣṇīṣa.
Place Subhūti on the left and Ānanda on the right.
Place the alms bowl in the southwest corner;
place the mendicant’s staff in the northwest corner; place Hārītī on the right side and Aparājitā on the left side.
"Place the 'Accomplisher of All Deeds' outside the maṇḍala; place a wheel in the center;
and upon it, place the object to be accomplished or the deity."

"In the outer courtyard, establish the gates of the eight directional deities; on both sides, place the nāga kings Nanda and Upananda. Invite each with their respective root mantra, or invite them all together with the heart-mantra of the family (*kula-hṛdaya*). Perform offerings according to the ritual rules, and thereafter perform *homa* for these various honored ones."

Either place the seal (mudrā) or arrange the seat; having purified the fire with the root mantra, perform one hundred and eight *homa* offerings of ghee and honey. Furthermore, using curd-cakes and sesame seeds, perform one hundred *homa* offerings for each with their respective root mantras. When these matters are completed, recite [the mantra] another one hundred times. This is the secret method for rectifying transgressions.

"All items offered must be fragrant and delicious; the food presented should consist of *uṇḍeraka* rice mixed with sugar and curd. By performing this rite, all the Honored Ones will be fully satisfied and delighted, and one will swiftly attain accomplishment."

Not only should one repair what is deficient, but one should also, every half-month, on festival days, or even daily, construct this maṇḍala to make offerings to the various deities; by doing so, all will become abundant and one will swiftly attain accomplishment.
If one is unable to do so at those times, one should perform it according to one's capacity.

"As previously described for the Buddha-family maṇḍala ritual, this Lotus-family ritual is likewise identical; one need only change the circle into a square, and its dimensions may be according to one's preference."
Place Avalokiteśvara in the center;
place Hayagrīva on the right side and Viśvarūpa on the left side; place the Three-Eyed One on the right side and the Four-Armed One on the left side.
On the right side place the Six-Armed One; on the left side place the Twelve-Armed One. On the right side place the Fulfiller of All Wishes (*Sarvārthasiddhi*).
Furthermore, on the right side place Yamāntaka, and on the left side place Mahāśrī;
on the right side place Tārā, and on the left side place Caṇḍaroṣaṇa near the door.
To the right, place Śvetā; to the left, place Cakrāravasinī; in the center, place a lotus; and outside the maṇḍala, place the deity of the family who accomplishes all activities.
This is the ritual for the Lotus Family’s *maṇḍala* for supplementing deficiencies.
"As previously described for the Buddha Family *maṇḍala*, this Vajra Family [maṇḍala] is likewise; however, it must be made square, and its dimensions may be according to one's preference."
On the east and west sides, place the Vajradhara;
on the right side, place the Vidyārāja, and on the left side, place Mañjughoṣa;
on the right side, place the wrathful Krodha-Śamkara, and on the left side, place Vajrāṅkuśa.
On the left side place Daṇḍa; on the left side place Mahābala;
on the right side place Muṣṭika;
on the right side place Śumbha, and on the left side place Tivaraka.
On the right side, place the *Ghaṇṭānirghoṣa*; on the left side, place the Wrathful Fire-Head (*Krodhāgnimūrdhan*).
Near the door on the left, place the Vajra-Fearsome-Eye (*Vajrabhairvanetra*);
near the door on the left, place the Vajra-Unconquerable (*Vajrāparājita*).
Outside the maṇḍala, place the deities of the primary family who are capable of accomplishing all tasks.
All other outer enclosures and methods of offering are as previously described.
This is the method for supplementing deficiencies in the Vajra Family.

"Having thus completed the offerings, one should pray for auspicious dreams. At dawn, having bathed and put on clean white garments, one should offer rice blossoms, blue *kubjaka* grass, and fragrant white flowers upon the ground where the maṇḍala was prepared; thereafter, one should smear it all over with cow dung and sweep it clean."

"Furthermore, perform three *pauṣṭika* homas. Place curd, *kuśa* grass, ghee and honey, sesame seeds, and all other materials for the homa on the right side; place the vessel of *arka* water on the left. The ladle for the clarified butter (*ājya*) should be placed in front, separated by the clarified butter, and the vessel should be placed in front of the ladle. Use the *Sarvakarmaprasādhana-mantra* to sprinkle those items."
The lords of the various families are installed and offered worship; using their respective root mantras, one invokes their principal deities and likewise installs them.
One places ghee in front of oneself;
in front of the ghee, one places fire.
Place the object to be accomplished between the ghee and the fire.
First, [place] oneself;
next, the ghee.
Next, the objects;
then fire;
next, the Principal Deity and the Family Lord.
One should understand that the five aforementioned items are to be placed in the following order:
to the left of the Lord of the Family, place the *Tijaṇimaṃtra*; to the right, place the *Sarvakarmasādhaka*, arranged in the sequence as previously described in the *homa* ritual.

"First, spread out blue kuśa grass, place cakes mixed with curd, scatter rice-grain flowers, and present the bali offering; then, make offerings of fine and beautiful incense, and subsequently perform the homa rites according to the ritual rules."
The accomplished object should be placed in a vessel made of gold, or silver, or refined copper, or stone, or conch, or shell, or wood, or a vessel of *vālmīka* clay.
Upon the leaves, place a vessel, or spread out leaves from a milky tree;
or leaves from an *argha* tree;
or leaves from a plantain tree.
Alternatively, one may use lotus flowers or lotus petals;
or one may take fresh, clean white cotton cloth and spread it out as appropriate.

Furthermore, one should first spread five layers of leaves upon the ground and place the object of accomplishment thereon, then cover that object with another five layers of leaves; or alternatively, these may be scattered.
Whether it be various garments or miscellaneous items, one should first understand the vessels in which they are contained.

Then, with an undistracted mind, perform the *pota* rite; illuminate the objects with the light of the mind and sprinkle them. Holding a ladle, slowly draw up the clarified butter (*sarpis*) and place it over the objects while reciting the root mantra. Upon reaching the syllable "Sva," pour it into the hearth; upon uttering the syllable "Ha," touch the objects again and return to the vessel of clarified butter.
In this manner, the contact with objects at the three locations—past, future, and present—must not be interrupted; this is called the *tripatā homa* method.
One should perform it one thousand times or one hundred times, or according to whether the mantra is extensive or abbreviated.
Alternatively, one may perform the movement up and down and the repetition [of the mantra] up to twenty-one times for the homa; this is called the limit of the total number of recitations.
During the *tripāda* (three-quarter) time, one should moisten the substance thoroughly with the ladle so that it becomes completely saturated.
When first placing the objects, first sprinkle them with water; next, press down upon them while reciting the mantra;
next, examine them;
and finally, present the offerings.
When the *homa* is completed, one must likewise proceed as follows.

Regarding the three signs of accomplishment described in the context of the *sādhana-maṇḍala*, if any such sign is perceived while performing this rite, one must immediately observe the prohibitions; it should be known that accomplishment will be attained before long.
If the substance is large, place it on the right side; if it is something to be held with the left hand, place it on the left side and sift it three times.
If one is performing the rite for the sake of accomplishing a sentient being, fashion its image and perform the homa while touching its head with the ladle;
if one desires to accomplish oneself, perform the homa by touching the crown of one's own head with the ladle.
If one performs the *bali* offering for the sake of another, one should simply utter that person's name while performing the *homa*.
Furthermore, there are three distinctions regarding the objects of accomplishment:
first, merely uttering the name; [the other two are as follows:]...
Second, one covers it with an object;
third, one leaves it exposed so that it may be seen by the eye.
In all such cases, one performs the homa using ghee.
If ghee is not available, one should use cow’s milk;
or use milk mixed with ghee;
or use the three sweets.
Alternatively, one should employ curd for the specific accomplishment of the visualization;
perform the homa as described in the original text;
or perform the homa with sesame seeds and ritual weapons.
If one is accomplishing a *vaidāra* [siddhi], one should perform homa with the heartwood of a hard-wooded fragrant tree;
or use storax and other such incenses as alternatives;

or, observing the specific distinctions of the object and the distinctions of the accomplishment, one should take various types of fragrant substances that correspond to the rite and perform the homa.
If one has prepared dog meat, one should likewise use its fat; the same applies to all other types of meat.

As for the substances to be accomplished, they may be placed entirely before [the practitioner]; using this *sarpata* method, one should explain the rite of *homa*. One should extensively perform the *sarpata* *homa* with those substances, and having done so, one will swiftly attain accomplishment.

"Having thoroughly washed and rinsed the *tripaṭa* cloth until it is pure, one should then perform the consecration according to the ritual rules. Once this is completed, one should offer worship and maintain the cloth before the *iṣṭadevatā*. Furthermore, one should present various kinds of food and drink as offerings to the *iṣṭadevatā*, and also perform sacrifices to the world-protectors (*lokapāla*) of the eight directions; these must likewise be offered at the site of the *homa* according to the ritual rules."

Thereafter, on the eighth day, one should bathe according to the ritual using various cleansing powders and *āmala* fruit. At the hour of midday, one should press the object with the hand while performing recitation. Furthermore, one should separately prepare a thread and, following the previous procedure, perform the recitation upon it; likewise, for the armlet, the garment, the ashes, and the mustard-water, each must be consecrated through recitation as previously described.

"When one wishes to perform an accomplishment (*sādhana*), these articles for protecting the body must first be consecrated through recitation to be used later. By thus reciting over the various articles that protect the body, they will all prove effective whenever they are employed at the time of accomplishment."
Therefore, one must first perform recitations in advance and prepare offerings such as flowers; furthermore, one must perform ritual recitations while placing these items nearby.

Next, one should construct a maṇḍala according to the rules and perform the rites of accomplishment (*sādhana*), reciting the *Sarvakarmaprasādhinī* mantra. One should wrap the five-colored boundary lines around four stakes, reciting the *Kumārakrodha* (Muñjakeśvara) mantra over them. Place the ritual vases before the outer gate; the two ends of the wrapped lines should both be tied to the necks of the vases, leaving them sufficiently loose. Whenever entering or exiting, one should keep Kumārakrodha in mind and pass through the line by lifting it.
It may also be accomplished by reciting the mantra of Kuṇḍalī,
or by reciting the mantra of one's own root-practice (mūlamantra).
As previously explained regarding the method for dispelling obstacles, one must first purify the site and then perform the ritual.
"At that time, perform external offerings to the world-protecting deities (*lokapāla*) of the eight directions along with their retinues. Upon the vase, place a *vajra* or a branch bearing fruit;
then, either recite the mantra of the *vidyārāja* of the relevant family, or the *hṛdaya* of the family, or the *mātṛkā* of the family, to protect that location."
Alternatively, one may place the various mudrās belonging to their respective sections in their original directions to ward off all obstacles.

As for the stakes, one should recite the Vajrakīla mantra over them one hundred times; having fashioned the upper end of each stake into a three-pronged vajra, one should drive them into the four corners outside the purified ritual chamber.
If one drives [stakes] into the corners of the boundary lines of the maṇḍala, this is called the Vajrakīla rite, which is capable of accomplishing all tasks.
That maṇḍala may be made either with powdered dry pigments or with various kinds of powdered incense.

Alternatively, one may use moist pigments and a brush made of cow hair to draw a three-pronged vajra outside each corner; all the boundary lines should likewise be formed into the shape of three-pronged vajras, while reciting the Vajraprākāra mantra over them.
Furthermore, within that vajra-shaped boundary, one should again place a vajra horizontally; this should be done throughout.
This is called the Vajra-railing, and one should recite the Vajra-railing mantra over it.
Having performed this, nothing can destroy it; therefore, one should perform the rite of accomplishment therein, placing a *vajra* at each of the gates and outside the gates.
"As for the method of accomplishment, one may perform it either in a pure chamber or in the open air;
the maṇḍala should measure five cubits, or seven, or eight.
Alternatively, one should observe the specific matter to be accomplished and construct it according to the size of that matter."
“Place a *vajra* in the center of each gate, and place vases at each corner;
place the vase that accomplishes all tasks (*sarvakarmika-ghaṭa*) in front of the outer gate.
Place the seal of the Dharma wheel (*dharmacakra-mudrā*) in the east and west within.”
On the right, place the seal of Buddhalocanā; on the left, place the seal of the ūrṇā-kośa (the hair-treasure).
On the right, place the seal of the tusk; on the left, the seal of Śakti.
On the right, place the five kinds of Buddha-uṣṇīṣas, arranging them in sequence on both the left and the right.

Within the Buddha Family, all the deities are to be arranged at will in order on the left and right; finally, Ānanda and Subhūti are placed at both sides, and next, near the entrance, Ajita is placed.
"Next, place the Vidyārāja Siddhārtha on the eastern side of the outer enclosure;
place Mahāsthāmaprāpta on the northern side;
and place Mañjuśrī on the southern side."
On the western side, place the Honored One Mahātejas;

on the eastern side, to the right, place Brahmā and the various devas of the Form Realm (rūpadhātu), and to the left, place Indra up to the King of Paranirmita-vaśavartin, as well as the terrestrial deities.
"In the southeast, place the Fire God with the various ṛṣis as his retinue;
in the south, place King Yama with the piśācas, bhūtas, and mātṛs as his retinue;
in the southwest, place the deity Nirṛti with the various rākṣasas as his retinue."
At the western gate, place the deity Varuṇa with the hosts of nāgas as his retinue;
at the northern side of the gate, place the Earth Deity with the asuras as his retinue;
and in the northwest, place the Wind Deity with the garuḍas as his retinue.
In the north, place the Heavenly King Vaiśravaṇa with the yakṣas as his retinue;
in the northeast, place the deity Īśāna with the kumbhāṇḍas as his retinue.
Furthermore, at another location on the western side, place the Sun Deity (Sūrya) together with the planetary deities;
at yet another location on the western side, place the Moon Deity (Candra) surrounded by the lunar mansions (nakṣatras);
and on both sides of the bend of the western gate, place the Nanda and Upananda Dragon Kings.

"Place all the mantras and vidyās of the messengers and their like belonging to the Buddha Family on the four sides of the outer enclosure as you wish; thereafter, according to the ritual, invoke them and perform the offerings, homa, and recitation in sequence."

In the very center, one should install the principal deity or the object of accomplishment. Just as the rites for protecting the body and so forth are explained in the *maṇḍala* rituals, these should likewise be performed in their proper sequence. This is the *maṇḍala* ritual for accomplishing all objects of the Buddha Family; no obstacles whatsoever can find an opportunity there, and by performing the rite within it, one will swiftly attain accomplishment.
"All the honored ones shall increase their protection. Previously, one constructed a maṇḍala using five colors; here, however, change the circle into a square.
Within its inner court, place the lotus seal at the center of the eastern side."
To the right, place the Seven Tārā Vidyās; to the left, place the Seven Auspicious Vidyās.
Next, place the Six Great Vidyārājas to the left and right;
to the right, place Pañjaranābhasiddhi, and to the left, place Khagarbha-mati.
On both sides near the gate, place one Vajraśṛṅkhalā and one Hayagrīva; in front of the outer gate, place the *sarvakarmaprasādhaka-kalaśa* (the vase that accomplishes all activities);
at the gates and corners, place vajras; and in the center, place a lotus.

"In the outer enclosure, place Brahmā, Indra, Maheśvara, and so forth; the gods of the Śuddhāvāsa heavens; the Bodhisattvas Vimalacaryā, Prabhāmandita, Vyūharāja, and Anantanāgarāja; the Nāga kings Śuṇḍara and Upaśuṇḍara; and the Vidyādhara King Khañjarīṭa together with all the other Vidyādharas, as before."
Within this section, one may place at will all the messengers, mantras, and vidyās belonging to the World-Protectors (Lokapālas) of the various directions.

The sequence for their placement is exactly as previously described; thus, no obstacles whatsoever shall find an opportunity to prevail, and one should perform the rites of accomplishment (*sādhana*) therein.
"As previously described, construct the boundary lines as before.
Within the inner court, place Susiddhikara on the eastern side;
to his right, place the Vidyārājñī Vajragāndhārī, and to his left, place the Vidyārājñī Vajraśṛṅkhalā."
To the right is placed the Vidyārāja Śumbha, and to the left is placed the Vidyārājñī Kṛtī;
to the right is placed the Honored One Vajra, and to the left is placed Vajradaṇḍa;
to the right is placed the Vajramātṛ-gadā, and to the left is placed Vajrasaṃkara.
To the right, place the Vidyārājñī Vajrāṅkuśī; to the left, place the Vidyārājñī Māmakī.
On the eastern side of the outer enclosure, place the messenger Prajñākūṭa, the messenger Vajraprajña, Maheśvara and his consort, and the Heavenly King Vaiśravaṇa along with the yakṣas.
In front of the outer gate, one should prepare the various ritual vessels.

Within the Vajra Family, all the mantras and vidyās of the messengers (dūtas), as well as the bhūtas, piśācas, gandharvas, mahoragas, and vidyādharas, and the world-protectors of the eight directions, should be installed in their respective courtyards in order. Thereafter, having invited them, one should perform the offerings according to the rite, and commence the homa, recitation, and the rites for accomplishment.

Regarding the deities to whom one makes the invocation, one should employ the mantras of the Vidyārājas or the mantras of the Kulas (Buddhamātṛs) to invite all the deities present within the maṇḍala; this act is called "placing the vases. Just as with the qualifications for the ritual procedures in the aforementioned maṇḍala, so too are all the procedures for this method of accomplishment.

"If one performs the rites of accomplishment within these maṇḍalas, one shall attain siddhi even if one does not possess the methods for protecting the body; for those deities have their own solemn vow:
'If anyone invites us to the maṇḍala and makes offerings according to the Dharma with a sincere heart, we shall grant them whatever they seek.'"
Therefore, one should know that in this regard there will be no obstacles and protection will certainly be granted.

If one employs the Family Heart-mantra (*kula-hṛdaya*), the Family Mother (*kulamātṛ*), or the Vidyā Consort, as well as the mantras capable of accomplishing all tasks and the Family Body-protection mantra (*kāyarakṣā*) to perform the invocation, the various realms of body-protection will swiftly attain accomplishment.
This is the secret dharma of the three families.

Furthermore, regarding the explanation of the secret maṇḍalas common to the three families: one should place the vajra upon the path of the dharmadhātu; in the center, place the mudrā of the presiding deity of the family; and before that, place the presiding mantra-lord. Alternatively, as previously described, one may place a kalaśa (vase) there, filled with substances such as those contained within vessels, and set it upon the [central] vase.
"In the eastern side of the inner court, place the seal of the Tathāgata;
in the northern side, place the seal of Avalokiteśvara;
and in the southern side, place the seal of Vajra."
On the right side of the western face, place Rudra;
on the left side, place the Heavenly King Vaiśravaṇa.

Just as previously explained for the Maṇḍala of the Vidyārājas, these should also be installed in this same sequence: on the right side, place the Family Mother Vidyā; on the left side, place the Activity-performing Vidyā. It is the same for the two families of Padma and Vajra on the left and right.
On the right side facing west, recite "Kṣa-ri," and place "Lakṣmī" on the right.
Place the alms-bowl (*pātra*) and the *cīvara* at the two corners of the east and west;
place the *daṇḍa* staff and the water flask (*kuṇḍikā*) at the two corners of the north.
At the two corners facing south, place a *vajra* and a *khaṭvāṅga*;
at the corner facing west, place a wheel and a precious vase.
Outside the gate, establish a separate location and place the Aparājita there.
In front of the eastern gate, place Hārītī;
in front of the southern gate, place Kūṭadharīka;
and in front of the northern gate, place Icāketaka.
In the outer enclosure, one should place various mudrās at will and perform the ritual invocation and offerings according to the dharma; this is the secret universal maṇḍala.
Whatever substances for accomplishment are prepared within it will all attain siddhi; even Māra cannot find an opportunity there, let alone other vināyakas.

One should offer various fragrant flowers, lamps, and diverse foods while reciting mantras to make them radiant, and then perform the offering; as it is taught regarding offerings for recitation and for the maṇḍala, so too should this be done.
If performed within a purified chamber, it is likewise the same; however, the various offerings to the lord of the maṇḍala should be increased fourfold—this is the secret method.

"Once the offerings have been completed, one should next perform the ritual sacrifice outside in accordance with the Dharma. Light lamps with ghee, using fresh and pure wicks to make offerings to the Principal Deity; each and every item must be presented along with argha water."
If one is performing the ritual for the *sādhya* deity, they will swiftly obtain results.

By reciting the mantra of a Vidyārāja while holding white mustard seeds, or using a mantra capable of accomplishing all tasks, or by reciting a mantra for which one has previously attained mastery, and approaching the object to be accomplished, all obstacles will be dispelled and immediately retreat.

Furthermore, place the primary mudrā of the root deity on the left side, or simply hold and recite the Great Power mantra while placing it on the left; then, station a male figure at each of the eight directions.
First, in the east, that person is arrayed in the attire of Śakra, holding a vajra, with form and color exactly like Śakra;
in the south, that person is arrayed in the attire of Yama, holding a *daṇḍa* staff;
in the west, that person is arrayed in the attire of a Nāga King, holding a noose.
In the north, the person assumes the attire of Vaiśravaṇa, holding a staff with a skull-topped head;
in the northeast, the person assumes the attire of Īśāna, holding a trident;
in the southeast, the person assumes the attire of Mahādeva, appearing like a ṛṣi, and holds a water flask (*kamaṇḍalu*) and a rosary.
In the southwest, that person is dressed in the attire of a rākṣasa king, holding a horizontal sword in hand;
in the northwest, that person is dressed in the attire of a wind deity, holding a bannered flag in hand.
“Śakra is white; Yama is black; the Nāga King is red; Vaiśravaṇa is golden; Īśāna is white; Agni is the color of fire; the Rākṣasa King is the color of a pale black cloud; and Vāyu is blue.”
The garments they wear shall likewise be so.

These individuals must all receive the precepts and maintain them with extreme purity; they must possess great courage and bravery, be skilled in the methods for protecting the body, and have upright features, being in the prime of youth and robust in physique. The weapons they carry must all be consecrated through recitation; they must wear flower garlands interlaced across their necks and both shoulders, be prepared with white mustard seeds, and be well-versed in the signs of obstacles.
"If obstacles arise, one should immediately scatter white mustard seeds and strike them with them, or throw a garland of flowers;
or, if the obstacles are numerous and manifest great terrors, one should brandish the weapons one holds at them from a distance."

If they should press him closely and strike with weapons, he should scatter white mustard seeds and throw flower garlands while brandishing his own weapons; at the time of being struck, he must not move from his original position. If he moves from his original position, they will gain the advantage; therefore, he ought not to move from his original position.
"Among all the protective mudrās contained within this treasury, one should take those that are difficult to subdue and, having recited them and made offerings, place them by one's side.
If extremely fierce and harmful malevolent spirits should approach, one should personally strike them with those various mudrās;

or else, using white mustard seeds scattered while reciting the mantras that have previously been empowered through recitation, one should strike the malevolent ones. If they still do not cease, one should go outside and perform a ritual sacrifice for those troublesome hosts according to the Dharma, providing excellent food and drink in great abundance."
“There are, in total, nine kinds of universal protection for the Dharma.

Namely: warding off all obstacles; binding the boundary of the earth; binding the boundary of space; binding the boundary of the maṇḍala; binding the boundaries of the directions; binding the vajra wall; binding the vajra railing; protecting objects; and protecting the body to eliminate all malevolent influences.”
When performing the rite of accomplishment, one must keep such dharmas as these in mind.
"Alternatively, if one cannot provide the protective weapons for the respective directions, one should place the weapons appropriate to those directions;
if even this cannot be arranged, one should place nārāca weapons in all directions."
Alternatively, one may draw a bow and nock an arrow, placing them in various locations;

or provide assistance to those who accomplish the rite, being clearly versed in the *piṭaka* teachings, possessing wisdom and skillful means, having merit from recitation, maintaining pure conduct, and standing at the entrance to assist with all matters and expel all malevolent influences—even within the inner and outer courtyards, they should all provide such assistance.

"All necessary matters must be fully prepared by evening; as soon as the sun has set, one should immediately begin the rite of accomplishment (*sādhana*). When feeling fatigued during the interval, one should go outside the maṇḍala, take water in the mouth to rinse it, and recite the mantra of Kuṇḍalī three handfuls.
Alternatively, one may recite the heart-mantra of one's chosen deity (*iṣṭadevatā*) and drink a small amount of cow’s ghee; all exhaustion shall thereby be cured.

Furthermore, mixing long pepper (*pippalī*) with honey, one should recite the vidyā of the Mother of the Buddha Family (*Buddhakulamātṛ*) and apply it to the eyes; if one is drowsy and finds it difficult to rise, this shall immediately cure it."

"First, with a sincere heart, stand facing east and observe the various deities while offering refuge and making supplications. Among the three kinds of auspicious omens, whichever sign you perceive, perform the accomplishment (*sādhana*) with a joyful mind; as the initial omen was perceived, so too shall the accomplishment be realized."

Therefore, the practitioner should observe the preliminary omens; first, one must for a brief moment contemplate the Vidyārāja Susiddhikara, and next, circumambulate the various ritual vases to the right.

When entering the maṇḍala, one should circumambulate every flask encountered, keeping them to the right. Upon arrival, one prostrates to the Honored One and gazes upon him; then, each flask is offered arghya with its respective root mantra, or else with the heart-mantra of the family.
One should summon the various lords of mantras with the mantras of the vidyārājas;

once the lords of vidyās have been summoned, one should visualize their respective mudrās and recite their fundamental mantras and vidyās, or simply visualize a single universal mudrā while reciting those mantras and vidyās. If one acts in this manner, one will swiftly attain siddhi.
"As for the objects to be accomplished, they may be placed within an *argha* vessel, or set upon a flask;
or they may be held within cupped hands,
or merely brought to mind through mental recollection."
Either place it in a vessel made of *bālamuka* wood, or upon a leaf,
or before the inner principal deity.
"Smear all the vessels to be prepared with ox-gall;
next, perform protection using white mustard seeds;
then, recite the mantra while making offerings of marica flowers to the objects."
By applying ox-gall, one achieves the state of being restrained;
by using mustard seeds, one achieves protection;
and by offering flowers, one must achieve radiant manifestation. These three methods should be performed in their proper sequence and must not be neglected or obstructed.
“Place the articles for accomplishment before the deity, ensuring that no other objects intervene between them.
These articles for accomplishment should be protected by means of two methods: first, the mudrā;”
2. White mustard seeds:

Because they cause the object to be accomplished to manifest signs of efficacy swiftly, one should repeatedly offer *argha*, flowers, incense, and other requisites, as well as curd. One should also frequently make offerings to those who assist in the accomplishment, so that they may protect the object and remain constantly at that location.

"Once the articles for offering have been thus arranged, one should then press them with the hand or gaze upon them with the eyes; with an undistracted mind, one should slowly recite [the mantra], repeatedly manifesting the splendor of the objects throughout the process."

In this manner, one should continue the recitation throughout the night without interruption. During the three periods of that night, one should perform offerings in succession with *argha* water and other substances.

If it becomes necessary to go outside to rinse the mouth, one should have an assistant take the seat in front and continue the recitation in sequence; whatever the practitioner may forget or omit, the assistant must ensure it is all made up.
"When reciting, if great malevolent spirits arrive, those assisting in the practice should repel them;
if they cannot be restrained, the practitioner should personally scatter white mustard seeds to ward off the calamity."

"When those who assist in the practice recite over the object, if a malevolent manifestation appears in the east in the form of a great thunderclap, one should know this to be the malevolence of Śakra."
In the southeast, this obstacle appears: a great being of fire-colored hue, or like the setting sun; one should know that this is the obstacle of the Fire God (Agni).

In the south, this malevolent apparition appears: in the form of a corpse, most terrifying, crying out with a loud voice, holding a great sword in hand and having all their noses cut off, holding skulls filled with human blood which they drink while flames burn upon their heads; one should know that this is the malevolence of Yama.

In the southwest, this obstacle appears: namely, the raining down of excrement, urine, and filth upon the maṇḍala, as well as various other forms that are most terrifying; one should know that this is the nīlāṅga obstacle.
In the west, there appears this danger, namely the occurrence of rain, thunder, lightning, thunderbolts, hail, and so forth; one should know that this is the danger of the Dragon King.
In the northwest, there appears this danger, namely the rising of a great black wind; one should know that this is the danger of the Wind Deity.
In the north, there is this obstacle that manifests: namely, male yakṣas and female yakṣas who harass the practitioner; one should know that this is the obstacle of the Heavenly King Vaiśravaṇa.

In the northeast, these obstacles appear: namely, those with the heads of elephants, pigs, and dogs, each with a different form and holding a mountain of fire; one should know that these are the obstacles of Īśāna.
When various devas appear above, possessing great majesty and power, one should know that these are the devas of the upper direction.
When there is difficulty below, such as the earth shaking and splitting, one should know that these are the asuras.
"Only when the supreme accomplishment (*uttamasiddhi*) is being performed do such malevolent signs appear.

These and other such signs appear during the middle watch of the night; one should know that for ordinary, superior, and middling accomplishments, the signs of malevolence likewise increase in magnitude accordingly."
During the three periods of the night, these are the superior, middling, and inferior signs corresponding to their respective times; if they do not correspond, then accomplishment is not achieved.
These three types of signs—namely, the sign of warmth, the sign of vapor, and the sign of light—should appear in successive order.
If the highest accomplishment is attained, one possesses all three characteristics;
if the middling accomplishment is attained, one possesses the first two characteristics;
if the lowest accomplishment is attained, only the first characteristic is manifested.

Alternatively, if while reciting or reading with devotion, the three signs appear in succession during the first watch of the night, one should immediately restrain their light with the vidyā of the Mother of the Family;
restrain those signs with the heart-mantra of the Vidyārāja;
and apply powdered ox-gall by sprinkling it while reciting the mantra.
Some press with their hands;
some sprinkle with ghee;
some scatter flowers;
Alternatively, one may scatter white mustard seeds;
or simply sprinkle water to restrain its manifestation, whereupon it may be used immediately and its vow will likewise be fulfilled.

Or, if one restrains it during the first watch of the night, it may be used only when the appointed time arrives through the power of recitation; the methods for achieving success therein should be understood accordingly.
"In the first watch of the night, the lower siddhi is accomplished;
in the middle watch of the night, the middling accomplishment is obtained;
and when the dawn light appears, the supreme accomplishment is obtained."
Among these, for those who achieve success at midnight, once the ritual prohibitions have been observed according to the dharma, they may even enjoy the results until dawn;
the same principle should be understood to apply to the lower levels of achievement.
"If those who assisted at the time of its preparation do not enjoy it, it is not auspicious;

even if the substance has been prepared, if one does not immediately enjoy it and yet does not set it aside, and fails to enjoy it until the break of dawn, that substance will be like a withered flower or like foul food, unfit for use."
Because one has recited [the mantra], one invokes the mantra to enter into the object; yet once the time limit has passed, its efficacy is lost.

Furthermore, although signs of accomplishment may initially appear for an object, if it is not actually accomplished, one should at that time restrain those signs. Later, by performing rites such as radiating light, as well as making offerings and receiving empowerment on various festival days, one will then achieve accomplishment.
If, however, it is not accomplished after three years have passed, one should know that this object cannot be brought to fruition.
The highest level of accomplishment is limited to three years;
the middling level to six months;
as for the lowest level of accomplishment, there is no fixed time limit.
The ritual for recovering what has been lost is also like this.
Chapter Thirty-Seven: The Ritual for Recovering Stolen Accomplished Objects from the Susiddhikara Sūtra. "I shall now explain the ritual for recovering objects that have been stolen."
When the object has been completed, or at the time of performing the rite of accomplishment, the object may be stolen;
either its form is seen at the moment of theft, or the object is simply lost without the thief being seen.
At that time, without selecting an auspicious day or observing a fast, one should immediately perform this maṇḍala rite when anger arises, using triangular funeral ashes for its construction.
Open only the western gate; place the principal deity (mūlavidyā) in front of the outer gate, and place the Vidyārāja Susiddhikara at the eastern corner of the inner courtyard.
To the right, place Vajracanda; to the left, place Mahācanda.
To the left, place Vajramuṣṭi; to the right, place Vajrāṅkuśa.
To the right, place Vajrakīlikīla; to the left, place Vemacitrin.
To the right, place Revata; to the left, place Piṅgala.
To the right, place Aśvinī; to the left, place Śaṃkara.
To the right, place Viyaya; at the right gate, place Kali;
at the left gate, place Nandimukha; to the left, place Vajrasena;
and to the right, place Somahu along with all other great wrathful deities (*krodha*).

To bring about accomplishment, one should arrange the deities in their proper sequence and perform the invocation according to the ritual, making successive offerings of red flowers, red food, and so forth.

One should perform here the *ābhicāruka* rites as previously described; the principal deity stationed outside the gate should be worshipped according to the ritual with exquisite flowers and other offerings.

Furthermore, the deities of the eight directions and those of the respective families stationed in the outer enclosure, as well as all other messengers and honored ones, must likewise be worshipped in this manner.
"In the center, perform the homa rite; the hearth shall be triangular, exactly as described before. Use *śrīkhaṇḍa* (sandalwood) smeared with one's own blood to perform the homa;
alternatively, use *kṛtavedhana* wood or the remains of firewood used for cremating corpses to perform the homa.
Once the fire has been kindled, mix the ashes from the cremation of corpses with one's own blood and perform the homa."
Furthermore, one should perform homa by mixing together four substances—poisonous medicine, one's own blood, mustard oil, and red mustard seeds;
then, taking these same four substances and fashioning them into the form of a thief, one sits upon it and performs homa by slicing the pieces apart with the left hand.
If there is one who can subdue anger and is proficient in the Dharma, they should perform this rite.

When the thief, trembling with fear and terror, brings the stolen goods and personally delivers them, the practitioner should grant him fearlessness; at that time, one should perform the *śāntika* rite for him.
If one does not do so, he will die.
Alternatively, one may further increase the items to be offered and place them secretly before the Honored One.

Furthermore, if the articles for accomplishment have been stolen over a long period and one wishes to recover them, one should immediately construct this *Sarvakarmasādhana-maṇḍala* common to the three families, arranging it with the four directions and placing the seal of the Vidyārāja Susiddhikara at the center.

"On the southern side of the inner court, place Vajrakrodha, Mahākrodha, Māmakī, Vajrāṅkuśabhojana, Vajramuṣṭi, Vajrajvālā, Vajramātṛkā, Vajrabhairava, Vajraśaṅkhalā, Kīlikīla, Prajñāvajra, Aparājita, as well as all the great wrathful deities and all the messengers."
The mantra-lords of great majesty and power are to be installed in order in the south and west.

On the northern side of the inner court, one should install according to the Dharma, in their respective order, all the mantras and vidyās, as well as the various messengers: those who fulfill all wishes, Avalokiteśvara, Hayagrīva, the multi-faced and multi-armed, the manifestor of many forms, Yaśodharā, Mahālakṣmī, Raktāśmī, Śvetā, Pañjaravasinī, Tārā, Caṇḍālī, and Meru.

"On the eastern side of the inner court, place the various other *uṣṇīṣas* such as the *Suvarṇacakravarti-uṣṇīṣa*, as well as the *ūrṇā*, the *Buddhalocanā*, the *Buddhaśakti*, the Buddha’s tooth, the Buddha’s compassion, and the *Aparājita*, along with other principal *vidyās* and mantras capable of accomplishing all tasks, and all other mantras and messengers; arrange them each in their respective order according to the ritual rules on that eastern side.
Those situated near the outer gate should likewise be arranged according to the ritual rules as before."
Regarding the deities of the eight directions in the outer enclosure: place Brahmā and his retinue at the western gate;
at the northern side of the western gate, place Maheśvara together with his consort, Yanapadī, and their various attendants;
as well as the seven Mātṛkās, the eight Nāga Kings, and all their respective retinues.

The asuras and their retinues who have taken refuge in the Buddha, along with deities of great majesty and power, are each arranged in the outer enclosure according to the Dharma and in proper sequence; they are invoked with utmost sincerity and offered worship in successive order.

"To the west outside, place a homa fire pit; fashion an image of the thief out of wax and place it within a winnowing basket. Perform the invocation, sacrifice, offering, and homa according to the ābhicāruka rite;
then, cut the image with a blade and perform the homa."
Alternatively, one may perform it according to the *ābhicāruka* rites taught in one’s own *kula*;
or one may perform it in the same manner when the deity steals [the substance] itself or when it is accomplished even though not given.
From the fifth day to the fourteenth day of the dark fortnight, performing the ritual during this interval is said to be supremely auspicious.

Furthermore, one should employ various fierce methods such as striking with staffs, whips, or setting it ablaze; using the *mudrā* of the *vajrakīla*, one should pierce its body and smear it all over with blood, black mustard seeds, oil, and salt. One may inflict any desired suffering upon it and thus harm it;
furthermore, one should cover its form with a shroud used for corpses.

Bind it with a red thread, offer red flowers, and while reciting the mantra, wear it yourself and stare at it with a fierce gaze. Insert words of reprimand into the mantra and strike it every day; if the person brings an offering, then you should cease.
"In the middle of the night, one should perform this fierce rite: using *kumārī* oil mixed with black mustard seeds, perform a *homa* offering;
furthermore, combine poison, one's own blood, mustard seeds, oil, salt, and black mustard seeds, and while reciting the name of the thief who stole the goods, perform the *homa* eight hundred times;
or alternatively, simply mix one's own blood with salt and perform the *homa*."

"If such a bearer of suffering does not return the object, one should instead perform the 'Fierce Method until Death. One should carry out everywhere the methods of killing as taught in the *Abhicāruka* rites, inserting the words of killing into the mantra."
If someone brings an object and requests that the practice be ceased, one should grant them joy;
if they have already used the object and bring another to replace it, one should likewise cease the matter;
or if they have already used the object and have nothing to replace it, yet come to express regret and apologize, one should still cease the matter and bestow joy upon them.
If he should lose it or give it away to another, then regarding whatever remains that is brought back, one should cease the matter and bestow joy upon him.
One should perform homa with the Vajramantra;
or perform homa with Mahākrodha, or with Aśuci-krodha.
Alternatively, one may perform *homa* using the mantra for recovering lost items as taught in the specific section [of the ritual manual].
However, these three types of mantras are common to the mantras of all three families:

"Oṃ akṣaṇaye svāhā vighnāya svāhā. After the rite for the Fire Deity (*Agni*), take three round morsels of food; reciting the single-syllable mantra once for each, burn them and offer the three full round morsels as an oblation to the Fire Deity.
Furthermore, the homa mantra is as follows:
“Oṃ ajñāye ṣya ṣya vahanāya japi japi nibhaya svāhā. Then, taking one portion of ghee and reciting the vidyā once, burn it into the fire three times to make offerings to the Fire Deity.
The Vajra-family Wrathful Vajra Mantra:
"Oṃ kili kili vajra-krodha hūṃ phaṭ. With this mantra, perform the fire-offering rite (homa) by reciting it once for each oblation.
The mantra for accomplishing the homa rite is:
"Namo ratna..."
Natarājāya namaḥ śmaśānāya.
Vajrapāṇaye mahāyakṣasenāpateye.
Oṃ hāra hāra.
Vajramahāvajra!
Duna duna vajra.
dhā dhā vajra!
Vāpaka vāpaka vajra!
Nara nara vajra.
Narayana Narayana Vajra.
Mīnarāya mīnarāya vajra.
Cchinda cchinda vajra!
Pinadipinavajraḥ
"Hūṃ Phaṭ.
By reciting this mantra while performing the homa rite, one will swiftly attain accomplishment.
If one obtains the actual object or a substitute for it, one shall thereby protect that object as well as oneself.
On festival days, one should perform the rites of illumination and so forth in their proper sequence.
Among these, of the substances for accomplishment and the substances for minor accomplishments, one portion should be offered to the World-Honored One;
one portion should be offered to the Ācārya.
One portion is offered as a gift to those who have previously attained accomplishment;
one portion is offered to companions and others;
and one portion is taken for oneself and divided into two parts:
"One part is for one's own use, and one part is offered to the bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, upāsikās, and others.

This is the rule for all such residual items: first, offer arghya water to the Honored Ones and others, and afterwards take your own portion. For those items previously consecrated, divide them by offering arghya; take double their value for your own enjoyment, as 'value' here refers to the act of making an offering."
If the ācārya is not present, one may take back one's share and use it oneself; as for its value, the sense of shame and remorse that arises in one's mind is itself the value.
When exiting the maṇḍala to offer it to those who have previously attained accomplishment, one should speak these words:
"May those who have previously attained accomplishment receive their respective portions.
Holding the argha vessel in hand, one should thus chant a second and a third time.
"If there is no one to take it, you should immediately give it to your companions without harboring any doubt.

Because they possess a devout mind, because they make offerings, because they maintain the precepts, and because they serve as attendants, they are those who have already attained [merit]; therefore, they should receive their share."
After he has recited this three times, his companions should respond thus:
"We are indeed those who have previously attained accomplishment.
The practitioner shall then divide the objects among himself and his companions equally.
"If the substance is so small that it cannot be divided—such as *añjana* or cow bezoar (*gorocana*), which are indivisible—one should mentally determine its portion and then use it for oneself."
There are such objects that are for the use of a single person alone and cannot be divided, such as wheels, swords, and the like.
One should perform their accomplishment in accordance with what is taught in their respective original texts.
The painted scrolls, images, and so forth likewise must not be divided.
Regarding the articles for accomplishment in this primary rite, even if their quantity is small, one may increase them beyond the original measure as desired to achieve accomplishment.

One should perform the accomplishment together with companions, based on the proportions of the person who has already achieved it; even if one reduces these by half, accomplishment may still be attained.
Alternatively, one must practice according to the specific measurements prescribed in the root text of that particular method.
"When a traveler distributes goods to his companions, he should give instructions, saying:
'You shall follow my various commands.
Once they have given their assent, he should then provide them with the goods."
Whether it be when one person, having achieved benefit for others, relies on this treasury of teachings;

or when, within other dharmas, it is permitted that all items be shared with companions and the like—at such times, goods should be divided according to the limits of each person's contribution and labor, and one must not show partiality.

"Once the substances have been prepared, one should first make offerings to the *iṣṭadevatā*. Having generated deep shame and remorse, one should then respectfully request [the deity] once more before distributing them; this applies to all the rituals of every *kula*."

The middling and lower levels of accomplishment should be understood accordingly. One should give rise to deep shame and remorse, and offer respectful service and offerings; furthermore, regarding the movement and conduct obtained through the gift of material wealth, one should repay the value of that object by following the instructions given.

Once the object has been accomplished, first offer *argha* and distribute it according to the ritual rules. Recite the root mantra and perform the mudrā; contemplate the principal deity (*iṣṭadevatā*) with the mind and recite the mantras of the Vidyārāja and Vidyārājñī. Only after such contemplation should one enjoy the object. One will then be able to ascend into the sky at will to the abode of the various sages, where no one can destroy or despise them; even if there are enemies, they will be unable to cause harm.

"The practitioner who has achieved accomplishment must constantly mind the *iṣṭadevatā* (honored deity) and never let them be forgotten. One must always keep the articles of accomplishment in mind or gaze upon them with the eyes. For the sake of the mantra-dharmas of the Vidyārāja, one is revered by all sages; for the sake of the Vidyārājñī, there is no fear from any quarter. One must not neglect performing the *samaya-mudrā*, the *kula-mudrā*, or gazing at objects with the vidyā-mantra."
Upon meeting a rishi, one should first show respect and inquire:
"Welcome; are you at ease? Why have you come here?
One should respond with comforting words and gentle speech.

"When wandering through the air, one should not pass over a shrine, nor over a solitary tree, a crossroads, the dwellings of sages, a city wall, a sacrificial altar, an assembly place of Brahmins, or the abode of practitioners of heterodox paths; because of such overweening pride, one who passes over these will surely fall."
"Those who have fallen due to negligence should recite the mantras of the Vidyārājas and engage in contemplation;

if they have already fallen or are on the verge of falling, they shall immediately regain their original station in space. Although their physical form may change, the path is seen by the divine eye, just as a noble one reaches his destination as soon as he resolves his mind, or as one who remains unmoving in meditative concentration reaches it instantly."

Therefore, as they travel along that path previously perfected, by the power of their merit, garments appear spontaneously according to their wishes; they enjoy palaces, flowers, groves, gardens, and various birds; celestial maidens engage in play, song, dance, and music; and all manner of sensual pleasures blaze with radiant light, just like the wish-fulfilling jewel-trees at the beginning of an eon that can satisfy every aspiration.

For the sake of dwelling, there are gem-stone seats; beneath flowing channels, soft grasses carpet the ground; various necklaces serve as articles for physical enjoyment; auspicious trees bear ambrosial fruits; and even all places that one desires or recollects appear before one.

"Even though this is so, one must always protect oneself and not neglect this duty. One should dwell in pure groves, on mountain peaks, or on islands in the ocean, rivers, or sandbanks; for the sake of recreation, one should reside in such places, where there are the aforementioned sublime environments, or where one may dwell together with hosts of luminous immortals."

Chapter Thirty-Eight: The Chapter on the Ritual for Accomplishing the Full Array of Limbs. In the Susiddhikara Sūtra, Chapter Thirty-Eight: The Ritual for Accomplishing the Full Array of Limbs. "I shall now further explain the ritual for accomplishing *siddhi* through the complete array [of limbs].”

If the object is not accomplished, one should restrain it according to the rules, guard it, conceal it, or discard it; then, as before, perform the preliminary recitation rites and proceed again through to the rite of accomplishment.
If it is still not accomplished after doing so, one should redouble one’s diligence and once more perform the recitation and the rite of accomplishment.
If it is still not accomplished after seven such cycles, one should perform this rite, which will ensure certain accomplishment.
That is to say:
begging for alms, diligent effort, recitation, generating great reverence, and circumambulating and prostrating at the eight holy sites;
or alternatively, reciting the Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra seven times.
Alternatively, one may offer superior objects as gifts to the Saṃgha;
or by a river leading to the sea;

or on a sea island, one should construct one hundred stūpas. Before each stūpa, one should perform the ritual recitation according to the Dharma for one thousand times. If the final hundredth stūpa emits light, one should know that the rite has been definitively accomplished.

"Furthermore, construct one thousand stūpas and recite [the mantra] one thousand times before each one. Even if one has committed as many crimes of immediate retribution (ānantarya) as there are stūpas, once the count is complete, success will be naturally attained without further ritual performance.
Moreover, by reciting all mantras one koṭi times, they will certainly be accomplished.
If one performs the recitation for twelve years, even those with heavy sins will achieve success; even if the ritual requirements are incomplete, accomplishment will still be obtained."
Furthermore, once the number of recitations and the time have been completed, one should immediately perform the *vṛddhi-homa*;
or else, having constructed the *sarvakarmika-maṇḍala*, one should perform the four kinds of *homa* therein.
Either on a mountain peak,
or at a place where a herd of cattle previously resided,
or on an island in the Ganges; having leveled the ground there to construct a maṇḍala measuring one hundred and eight cubits, one should place one hundred jars.

At each of the four gates, pillars were erected to form the gateways, and before each gate a jeweled terrace was constructed, adorned with various ornaments. Garlanded branches of exquisite flowers were fashioned and tied to the gate pillars and the corner banners, completely surrounding the site. One hundred and eight lamps filled with ghee were arranged upon the maṇḍala, and one hundred and eight incense burners containing various famous incenses were also placed there.
One side of the inner courtyard measures seven cubits, one side of the outer courtyard measures three cubits, and the remainder is the center.
All invocations, offerings, and so forth are to be performed exactly as previously described, according to the homa ritual.
"Next, one should explain the specific procedure for the center: place the root mantra within a *kalaśa* golden flask, and perform the *homa* rite at the four sides of that flask.
Within the inner court (*abhyantarāvaraṇa*), place all the deities of the Buddha Family on the eastern side;
place all the deities of the Lotus Family on the northern side."
On its southern side, place all the deities belonging to the Vajra family;
on the western side, place the god Rudra and Vaiśravaṇa, the Heavenly King of Abundant Hearing, together with their retinues.
As previously stated, if the deities such as the messengers cannot be accommodated within the inner court, they should be placed in the outer court.
The guardians of the directions and their respective retinues should each be placed in their original positions;
likewise, the lords of the three families, as well as Rudra and Vaiśravaṇa, should first be established in their respective locations.
Next, one should further place the vidyārājas, vidyārājñīs, and the mantras for accomplishing activities, along with all the messengers, arranging them in their proper sequence;
and in front of the outer gate, one should place the venerable Kuṇḍalī and the venerable Aparājita.

Having thus constructed the maṇḍala according to the ritual procedure, or having already done so, one should perform the sequence of invocation using the heart-mantra (*hṛdaya*) of the respective family and present the offerings. Then, one should perform the recitation (*japa*) in the four directions. Subsequently, at each of the four sides where the vases are placed, one should perform the homa rite within the corresponding family; this is called the "homa for the enhancement of the deities."
For the offerings and food, use *nāra* as the oblation.
Once the ritual procedures have been performed, all the deities will become empowered.
Having thus completed the recitation and *homa*, perform further *homa* with clarified butter using the mantra of the Family Mother (*kulamātṛ*).
Next, perform homa with milk-rice mixed with ghee using the mantra of the Buddha-Bhagavān;
further, perform homa with sesame seeds mixed with the three sweets using the mantra of the Family Mother (Kulamātṛ);
and again, perform homa with ghee using the mantra of the Family Mother.

Having performed this rite, one shall obtain all the Honored Ones; they will immediately be fully satisfied, and through the accomplishment of increase and perfection, they will all be delighted and swiftly grant success.
If one constructs this maṇḍala up to seven times, accomplishment is certain.

As previously described, while performing the recitation and circumambulating the eight stupas, if one constructs this maṇḍala up to seven times and yet does not achieve success, one shall then subdue the deity through the *ābhicāruka* rite of harsh treatment. One should fashion an image of the deity out of wax, take its mantra, and perform the recitation.

First, recite the mantras of the Family Mothers and the Vidyārājas; place the mantra of the Principal Deity in the middle. For the *abhicāruka* (subjugation) fire-sacrifice (*homa*), apply mustard oil to the image, which will then immediately become feverish with agitation.

If one subdues another who is possessed, such that the entire body is in pain, one may strike them with a whip or flowers out of anger; using the two aforementioned mantras, one performs this offering with a mind of wrath, just as one would punish a malevolent spirit—the ritual for punishing the *iṣṭadevatā* (honored deity) is likewise.
One must act according to these teachings and may not act arbitrarily.
If the Honored One comes to see you and grants you accomplishment, once your original vow is fulfilled, you should cease the previous activity and perform the śāntika rite.

Alternatively, having thoroughly mixed together poisons, one's own blood, sesame seeds, oil, salt, and red mustard seeds, perform a homa at midnight; at that time, the deity will cry out in terror, "Stop!
Stop! Do not do this!"
"Then [the deity] immediately grants the accomplishment.

If, after performing the ritual in this manner for three days, [the deity] still does not come to grant the accomplishment, one should again apply oneself with even greater vigor and, with a fearless mind, cut off one's own flesh and perform the homa three times. The tutelary deity will then appear to seek that person's favor, and whatever wish the heart desires shall be granted as an accomplishment."
If there are any deficiencies or transgressions, they shall be pointed out one by one.
Even if one has committed the five deeds of immediate retribution, if one performs the homa of flesh for nine nights, the deity will certainly come and grant accomplishment.
This is the method for engaging in a ritual contest with a mantra; one must protect the body according to the Dharma with a fearless mind before proceeding, for it will certainly not be in vain.
Once success has been attained, one should immediately perform the śāntika rite; if any transgressions have been committed, they must be rectified.

"Among all matters of accomplishment, this maṇḍala is supreme; by performing the three types of rites within it, one obtains the three types of fruits. Within it, one should perform all activities as well as homa."

One should subdue the *iṣṭadevatā* (honored deity) as one would subdue a malevolent spirit (*bhūta*). For every ritual offering, one must use fresh materials; the same applies to the substances for the *homa*. This practice must not be undertaken with negligence.

One must bathe until pure and protect the body according to the Dharma without being disrespectful. Only one who clearly understands the *piṭaka* teachings may employ this method to subdue the *iṣṭadevatā*; should one act contrary to this, one will surely bring harm upon oneself.
